articles.title: Democratic senator-elect calls Trump 'unserious fool' while defending combative political style
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed told Pod Save America that Democrats must treat Trump as an "unserious fool" and stop clinging to outdated political decorum.
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic senator-elect from Michigan, leaned into accusations of acting cocky on the path to victory over Republican candidate Mike Rogers, citing a need to push back on President Donald Trump's manner of communication during an appearance on "Pod Save America."

"Long ago, you predicted that you would win this race by seven points, which, at the time, seemed like a pretty cocky and ill-considered thing to say. Then you won the race by seven points. People are still calling you cocky," podcast host Jon Favreau said during his interview with El-Sayed.

"I think there is a responsibility that we have to engage with [Trump] as the unserious fool that he is," El-Sayed replied.

El-Sayed's response sheds light on his view of his own campaign and the tone that he believes Democrats need to adopt to counter Trump's presence in American politics. It also raises questions of whether El-Sayed's campaign strategies will yield results in Congress.

In his view, Trump has changed the style of acceptable communication. In turn, he accused Democrats of being hesitant to abandon a kind of decorum to fight fire with fire.

"I just think there's a responsibility for us to walk out of 'The West Wing' episode that our politics used to feel like and into the reality of where we are," El-Sayed said, referring to a television drama known for its idealistic portrayal of American politics.

"I say that because if you've ever watched a bully in a room, if you don't stand up to the bully, it's not like the bully will just go away. The bully just gets stronger."

During his campaign, El-Sayed repeatedly pointed a finger at Trump for, in his view, ushering in a new age of political rhetoric. But that view also preceded his Senate bid.

He once accused President Donald Trump of inciting terrorism in a 2020 interview, citing a foiled plot to kidnap Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.

"These are terrorists; we have to call them that. We have to recognize that that is what the face of terrorism looks like right now. We have to step up against it," El-Sayed said.

"We gotta ask: Why are these people getting radicalized? Well, there must be some radical, extremist cleric out there who may be tweeting up a storm about all the things that they think need to be done, like liberating Michigan."

Although President Donald Trump did not call for any kind of violence against Whitmer, El-Sayed said he believed the president was at least partially responsible, pointing to a tweet Trump had made six months before the discovered plot.

"LIBERATE MICHIGAN!" Trump wrote in a post on Twitter, the social media platform now known as X. The post was one of a series calling to "liberate" Virginia and Minnesota from COVID-19 restrictions imposed by Democratic governors.

According to FBI comments to local media, the plot originated before Trump's post.

Even so, El-Sayed called the posts emblematic of a cultural toxicity that had made violence more likely.

"The idea that people would threaten her safety because she was willing to stand up to keep us all healthy is, to me, the example of what the kind of toxicity that we see out of Donald Trump creates," El-Sayed said.

A spokesperson for El-Sayed did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether he believed in a red line for what kind of rhetoric Democrats should refrain from using.

Having won his U.S. Senate election , El-Sayed will be sworn into office Jan. 3, 2027, the start of the 120th Congress.

articles.title: Opinion - A ‘reverse-Ginsburg’ scenario could flip the Supreme Court without packing
articles.summary: In Henry VI, Shakespeare wrote, “Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends.” Many today would like to chisel those words above the doors to the Supreme Court...
articles.body:
In Henry VI, Shakespeare wrote, "Defer no time, delays have dangerous ends." Many today would like to chisel those words above the doors to the Supreme Court. Time and time again, justices waited too long for their own legacies.

For many conservatives, the decisive loss of both houses of Congress has created a true nightmare scenario in which two conservatives (Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito) could hand Democrats the opportunity to take control of the Supreme Court without having to carry out their court-packing schemes. Control of the court could now be lost by sheer attrition.

Timing has always been a looming question for justices who want to see their seats filled by like-minded jurists. However, it is difficult to walk away from being one of nine.

Some served beyond their own capabilities in clinging to the court, becoming befuddled and isolated with age. That was the case with iconic justices such as William Douglas and Thurgood Marshall.

Others stayed too long to guarantee the preservation of their own legacies. The most recent example is Ruth Bader Ginsburg. Some of us wrote for years that Ginsburg was risking her legacy by not retiring while Barack Obama was president. After President Trump replaced her with Justice Amy Coney Barrett, many liberals (who were consciously silent before her death) lamented her decision.

Now, conservatives worry they may face a double tap. For two years, there has been speculation that Thomas (78) and Alito (76) might retire to allow a Republican president and Republican Senate to select their successors. Both declined to do so.

If they were hoping for a two-year cushion, that window just closed with a resounding bang. Even if they were to resign in the next two years, it is unlikely that Trump could replace either with a conservative nominee.

With at least 54 Senate seats (and perhaps as many as 56), the Democrats do not fear defections from independent-minded senators like Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.). They will also cite the denial of a vote for Merrick Garland during the Obama administration as a justification for denying a vote to Trump nominees.

Even before the election, liberals had raised money to campaign against even prospective nominees for Trump.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris called for Democratic donors to oppose "additional justices" that might be nominated by Trump "before they happen." She praised the fundraising by Josh Orton, president of the dark-money group "Demand Justice." It was a notable endorsement, since Demand Justice was infamous for its campaign to get Justice Stephen Breyer to resign, including mobile billboards reading "Breyer, retire. Don't risk your legacy." Demand Justice has also pushed a radical agenda, including court-packing .

Of course, Breyer did resign, allowing Biden to replace him with Ketanji Brown Jackson, arguably the farthest-left justice to ever sit on the court.

As soon as the Democrats took control, the Senate Minority Leader (and possible incoming Majority Leader) Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) declared that they would bar "any crappy nominees," which was taken to mean any Trump nominee.

In fairness to Thomas and Alito, neither is diminished by age. Both have appeared in public and shown they are fully capable and effective. In the cases of Douglas and Marshall, they were eventually pressured to resign after they appeared on television and were clearly enfeebled.

The last two years have seen some of the most important opinions from Thomas and Alito in their careers on the court. Now, however, they could be looking at not two more years but six more years to wait for a Republican president if the midterms foreshadow the 2028 election.

If so, by the time a Republican could succeed such a Democrat, Thomas would be roughly 84 and Alito 82. And the Senate may not even then be ready to confirm like-minded successors.

The risk is tremendous. If their vacancies cause a reverse Ginsburg, the court would shift from a 6-3 majority favoring conservatives to a 5-4 majority favoring liberals.

Worse yet, in the calls to pack the court with a liberal majority, politicians and pundits often point to Biden-appointee Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson as the model. Jackson has been widely criticized for a radical jurisprudence that discards longstanding norms and doctrines, including by her two liberal colleagues.

Such a court would make court packing entirely unnecessary. The signature opinions of Thomas and Alito would likely fall in quick succession, from Thomas's gun rights decision in Bruen to Alito's abortion ruling in Dobbs.

Nevertheless, it is much to ask for two jurists to resign when they are both mentally and physically capable, particularly after rendering some of their most influential opinions in the last two years.

Some believe that justices should not engage in strategic resignations to shape the ideology of the Court. These justices, they reason, have a right to serve out their lifetime appointments as long as they can do the job. They can have a clear conscience serving as long as they are able, and leave their replacements to the will of the American people.

In any case, with less than six weeks left with a Republican Senate, the time has effectively run out for the retirement option in holding these seats for conservatives.

The irony is that these two justices can take considerable credit in the building of the conservative jurisprudence that has emerged in recent years on the court. They have shown great patience in building the authority to overturn longstanding cases, from Roe v. Wade to Humphrey's Executor . That legacy may now rest with their own longevity in the years to come.

articles.title: PP convoca 3,5 mil moradores para 2ª dose da vacina da dengue | G1
articles.standfirst: Imunizante é destinado a quem recebeu a primeira aplicação de um lote próximo ao vencimento. Intervalo recomendado entre as doses é de 90 dias.
articles.summary: Mais de 3,5 mil moradores de Presidente Prudente (SP) que receberam a primeira dose da vacina contra a dengue ainda precisam completar o esquema vacinal.
articles.body:
Mais de 3,5 mil moradores de Presidente Prudente (SP) que receberam a primeira dose da vacina contra a dengue ainda precisam completar o esquema vacinal.

A segunda aplicação está disponível para adultos imunizados em julho e agosto com doses de um lote que estava próximo do vencimento.

Segundo balanço da Secretaria Municipal de Saúde (Sesau), foram aplicadas 3.798 primeiras doses nesse público. Até sexta-feira (6), apenas 265 pessoas haviam recebido a segunda aplicação.

A vacina Qdenga, produzida pelo laboratório japonês Takeda, deve ser administrada em duas doses, com intervalo de 90 dias entre elas, conforme as orientações da fabricante.

Quem recebeu a primeira dose nos primeiros dias de agosto já pode retornar a uma unidade de saúde. Já as pessoas vacinadas nos últimos dias da campanha, na semana de 20 de agosto, devem conferir a data registrada na carteira de vacinação e procurar o serviço de saúde no dia indicado.

Além do público adulto contemplado pelo lote próximo do vencimento, a vacinação de rotina continua disponível para adolescentes de 10 a 14 anos em todas as unidades de saúde de Presidente Prudente.

Até o fim da última semana, foram aplicadas 2.082 primeiras doses nessa faixa etária. Já a segunda aplicação soma 1.744 imunizações.

articles.title: Lula: Reforma do Judiciário é urgente para recuperar credibilidade | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente afirmou que é dever dos agentes públicos atenderem ao desejo de mudanças da população e que os juízes devem ser isentos, éticos e livres de conflito de interesses e projetos de enriquecimento.
articles.summary: Em pronunciamento, Lula defendeu a reforma do Judiciário para combater a corrupção e reafirmou o compromisso com a responsabilidade fiscal e a redução dos juros.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) disse durante um pronunciamento em rádio e TV na noite deste domingo (8) que o Brasil precisa fazer uma reforma política e do Judiciário com "urgência".

O presidente também afirmou que é dever dos agentes públicos do país atender a esse desejo da população.

"É chegada a hora da Justiça brasileira recuperar a sua credibilidade. A atividade da magistratura precisa de juízes isentos, éticos e livres de conflito de interesses e projetos de enriquecimento. Com uma Justiça eficaz, poderemos encarar com mais rigor a corrupção, o crime organizado e sonegadores", afirmou Lula.

Durante o pronunciamento, o presidente disse também que se preocupa com a trajetória da dívida pública e com a taxa de juros e reafirmou que tem compromisso com a responsabilidade fiscal, sem detalhar como vai controlar os gastos do governo nem anunciar novas medidas fiscais.

"A trajetória da dívida pública e os juros altos me preocupam, por isso reafirmo meu compromisso com a responsabilidade fiscal, para viabilizar políticas sociais sustentáveis e a ampliação tão necessária do investimento. Todo esse esforço será feito preservando as regras fiscais", afirmou o presidente.

O presidente também afirmou que um dos principais objetivos do seu quarto mandato é levar os investimentos do Brasil para mais de 20% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB), em parceria com a iniciativa privada.

"Para tanto, vamos criar as condições para reduzir a taxa de juros", disse Lula.

Lula também criticou a atuação das big techs durante as eleições de 2026, que classificou como tentativa de interferência. O presidente afirmou que o processo vem acontecendo também em outros países.

"As chamadas big techs tentaram interferir no processo eleitoral brasileiro, dando milhões de visualizações a conteúdos com desinformação e fake news. Mas, com a participação popular, a verdade venceu a mentira", afirmou.

O presidente voltou a dizer que vai criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública, promessa que Lula tinha condicionado à aprovação da proposta de emenda à Constituição da Segurança Pública, aprovada pelo Senado Federal na terça-feira (3).

Como já havia sido aprovada pela Câmara dos Deputados, a proposta segue para promulgação pelo presidente do Congresso Nacional.

articles.title: Quaest: 62% reprovam ida de Flávio Bolsonaro para os EUA, e 56% acham que ele está fugindo da Justiça | G1
articles.standfirst: Ida do senador aos Estados Unidos chegou ao conhecimento de 89% dos brasileiros, percentual superior ao registrado em episódios recentes, como o escândalo do Banco Master.
articles.summary: Ida do senador aos Estados Unidos chegou ao conhecimento de 89% dos brasileiros, percentual superior ao registrado em episódios recentes, como o escândalo do Banco Master.
articles.body:
Flávio Bolsonaro desembarca em um aeroporto próximo de Miami em 28 de outubro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Eva Marie Uzcategui

Pesquisa Quaest divulgada neste domingo (8) aponta que 56% dos brasileiros acreditam que o senador Flávio Bolsonaro deixou o país após as eleições com o objetivo de fugir da Justiça. Outros 35% avaliam que ele foi para os Estados Unidos para evitar uma perseguição política.

➡️A Quaest ouviu 2.004 pessoas entre os dias 30 de outubro e 2 de novembro. A pesquisa tem nível de confiança de 95% e margem de erro de dois pontos percentuais.

A viagem teve ampla repercussão: 89% dos entrevistados afirmaram ter tomado conhecimento da ida de Flávio aos EUA .

Segundo o diretor da Quaest, Felipe Nunes, este foi o maior índice de conhecimento já registrado em pesquisas recentes, superando episódios como o escândalo do Banco Master, o caso envolvendo Alexandre de Moraes e Daniel Vorcaro e a reunião de Jair Bolsonaro com embaixadores em 2022.

Conhecimento da ida de Flávio Bolsonaro para os EUA. — Foto: g1

Conhecimento da Ida de Flávio para os EUA. — Foto: g1

Entre os entrevistados que souberam da viagem, 62% consideram que Flávio agiu de maneira errada ao deixar o Brasil. Para 29%, a decisão foi correta, enquanto 9% não souberam ou preferiram não responder.

Entre os eleitores que declaram voto em Flávio Bolsonaro no segundo turno, 32% consideram errada a decisão. Na direita não bolsonarista, esse percentual sobe para 45%. Já entre os bolsonaristas, apenas 5% reprovam a saída.

Decisão de Flávio de ir para os Estados Unidos. — Foto: g1

Ida de Flávio para os EUA - identificação política. — Foto: g1

A percepção de que Flávio deixou o país com o objetivo evitar uma perseguição política é mais forte entre os eleitores bolsonaristas.

Ainda assim, a direita se divide sobre as motivações do senador, inclusive entre os que votaram nele no segundo turno. Entre os independentes, apenas cerca de um terço acredita que Flávio deixou o país para evitar uma perseguição política.

Na sua opinião, por que Flávio saiu do país? — Foto: g1

A pesquisa também avaliou a tentativa de Flávio de se autoproclamar presidente após as eleições. Segundo o levantamento, 70% dos brasileiros tomaram conhecimento do episódio.

A reação foi majoritariamente negativa: 60% consideram que ele agiu mal diante do resultado eleitoral. O percentual é superior ao registrado pela Quaest em dezembro de 2022, quando o instituto avaliou a postura de Jair Bolsonaro após a derrota nas urnas.

Flávio também levantou dúvidas sobre o resultado da eleição, atitude desaprovada por 59% dos entrevistados.

Segundo Felipe Nunes, essa rejeição reflete a percepção majoritária de que as eleições foram limpas e justas. Apenas um terço dos brasileiros acredita que houve fraude no resultado, proporção semelhante à registrada em 2022.

Resultado das eleições em 2026. — Foto: g1

Flávio Bolsonaro deixou o Brasil após o ministro Alexandre de Moraes determinar que ele entregasse seus passaportes . Ele descumpriu a ordem e entrou por terra na Argentina, de onde embarcou em um avião particular para os Estados Unidos.

O senador é investigado no Supremo Tribunal Federal (STF) por suspeitas de irregularidades no financiamento de um filme sobre o ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro, chamado "Dark Horse", e de lavagem de dinheiro em negócios relacionados a casas de apostas cujo dono é Willer Tomaz, advogado e amigo de Flávio.

Uma das investigações apura se o senador teria usado uma casa de apostas para lavar dinheiro. Outra investiga repasses de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, para a produção de “Dark Horse”.

Em uma das apurações, sob relatoria do ministro André Mendonça, Flávio é investigado pela possível prática de crimes relacionados ao financiamento da produção do filme "Dark Horse", sobre a trajetória do ex-presidente Jair Bolsonaro.

A investigação mira repasses de Daniel Vorcaro, ex-dono do Banco Master, à produção.

Outra investigação que tramita no STF, sob relatoria do ministro Alexandre de Moraes, apura se o senador cometeu o crime de lavagem de dinheiro usando uma casa de apostas.

A Polícia Federal (PF) quebrou o sigilo telemático do advogado Willer Tomaz, amigo de Flávio, e encontrou e-mails que apontavam que o senador foi cadastrado como "usuário master" de uma conta bancária da empresa Alcazar Holdings, de propriedade de Tomaz.

A PF afirma no seu relatório que há "elementos indicativos de vínculo de controle ou propriedade de fato de Willer Tomaz sobre a Rede Loto", a primeira a obter autorização estadual da Loterj, no Rio de Janeiro, para explorar apostas esportivas de cota fixa no estado.

O mandato de Flávio como senador termina em 2027 e, com a derrota nas urnas, ele deixará de exercer um cargo público e, por isso, não terá mais foro privilegiado em razão do mandato de senador.

🔎 O chamado foro privilegiado, tecnicamente denominado foro por prerrogativa de função, é a regra que determina que determinadas autoridades sejam investigadas e julgadas criminalmente por tribunais específicos em razão dos cargos que ocupam. No caso de senadores, crimes ligados ao exercício do mandato são analisados pelo STF.

Mesmo assim, as investigações das quais é alvo podem permanecer no STF. Isso porque, em 2025, o tribunal decidiu que, quando o crime investigado tiver sido praticado durante o exercício do cargo e estiver relacionado às funções desempenhadas pela autoridade, o foro é mantido mesmo após o fim do mandato.

articles.title: Operação conjunta recolhe fios soltos em Presidente Prudente | G1
articles.standfirst: Ação está prevista para ocorrer na segunda-feira (9), próximo à Praça 9 de Julho, e envolve secretaria municipal, Procon, Energisa e 17 representantes de telefonia, internet e TV.
articles.summary: Uma ação para recolher fios soltos está prevista para segunda-feira (9), próximo à Praça 9 de Julho, em Presidente Prudente (SP).
articles.body:
Calçadão no Centro de Presidente Prudente (SP) — Foto: Arquivo/Secom

A Prefeitura de Presidente Prudente (SP) realiza na segunda-feira (9) uma força-tarefa voltada à fiscalização, alinhamento e retirada de fios soltos ou inutilizados na região central da cidade. O mutirão tem início previsto para as 7h e concentrará os trabalhos no trecho que vai da base da Polícia Militar, na Praça 9 de Julho, até o calçadão municipal

A intervenção busca eliminar cabos em desuso ou com fiação pendente que oferecem risco de acidentes e prejuízos no tráfego de pedestres, motoristas e motociclistas.

A operação reunirá equipes da Secretaria Municipal de Desenvolvimento Econômico (Sedepp), fiscais do Procon local, técnicos da concessionária de energia elétrica Energisa e representantes de 17 operadoras de telefonia, internet e televisão a cabo. Ao longo do trajeto, os técnicos farão inspeções minuciosas poste a poste para identificar linhas clandestinas ou abandonadas pelas prestadoras de telecomunicação.

A administração municipal lembra que as empresas que deixarem cabeamentos soltos ou irregulares nos postes da rede pública estão sujeitas a sanções e multas financeiras, conforme estabelecem as leis municipais 9.339/2017 e 10.433/2021. As companhias que não regularizarem a infraestrutura instalada na área central poderão sofrer autuações durante a própria vistoria.

articles.title: Ministro da Educação garante nova oportunidade em dezembro para estudantes que perderam Enem por questões climáticas | G1
articles.standfirst: Leonardo Barchini afirmou que o Inep observa as questões climáticas para dar nova chance aos que não puderam chegar aos locais de prova
articles.summary: Leonardo Barchini afirmou que o Inep observa as questões climáticas para dar nova chance aos que não puderam chegar aos locais de prova
articles.body:
O ministro da Educação, Leonardo Barchini, afirmou neste domingo (8) que estudantes impossibilitados de realizar a prova por questões climáticas terão uma nova oportunidade em dezembro.

A fala ocorreu durante a visita do presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a sala de monitoramento do Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep) em Brasília, onde técnicos da autarquia do Ministério da Educação, responsável pela aplicação do Enem, acompanham os processos logísticos em todo o Brasil.

"Todas as questões climáticas estão sendo observadas pelo Inep. Para aqueles que não conseguirem chegar por motivos climáticos a gente tem uma segunda aplicação no mês de dezembro", declarou o ministro.

Pela fala do ministro e segundo o edital que estabelece as regras do Enem de 2026, as provas desses alunos acontecerão nos dias 15 e 16 de dezembro, quando é realizado o Enem PPL, uma modalidade destinada a Pessoas Privadas de Liberdade e Jovens sob Medida Socioeducativa que inclua privação de liberdade.

O Enem 2026 ocorre entre 8 e 15 de novembro em todo o país. Neste ano, 5.055.818 pessoas tiveram suas inscrições confirmadas e estão aptas para fazer o exame.

O número é o maior desde 2020, quando quase 5,8 milhões de pessoas haviam se inscrito. No entanto, com a pandemia de Covid-19, o exame não aconteceu naquele ano e houve uma queda brusca no número de inscritos no ano seguinte.

A prova é composta por 90 questões objetivas (dividas entre Linguagens e Ciências Humanas) e uma redação. No próximo domingo (16), serão mais 90 questões (Matemática e Ciências da Natureza).

articles.title: Lula se diz preocupado com dívida e que vai cumprir regras fiscais | G1
articles.standfirst: Reeleito para o quarto mandato, Lula terá como desafio negociar com um Congresso mais à direita e conciliar as promessas de campanha com as restrições das contas públicas.
articles.summary: Lula destaca responsabilidade fiscal e controle da dívida pública como prioridades para atrair investimentos e reduzir juros em seu quarto mandato.
articles.body:
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) disse durante um pronunciamento em rádio e TV na noite deste domingo (8) que se preocupa com a trajetória da dívida pública e com a taxa de juros e reafirmou que tem compromisso com a responsabilidade fiscal, sem detalhar como vai controlar os gastos do governo nem anunciar novas medidas.

"A trajetória da dívida pública e os juros altos me preocupam, por isso reafirmo meu compromisso com a responsabilidade fiscal, para viabilizar políticas sociais sustentáveis e a ampliação tão necessária do investimento. Todo esse esforço será feito preservando as regras fiscais", afirmou o presidente.

O presidente também afirmou que um dos principais objetivos do seu quarto mandato é levar para mais de 20% do Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) os investimentos do Brasil , em parceria com a iniciativa privada.

"Para tanto, vamos criar as condições para reduzir a taxa de juros.", disse Lula .

O presidente também afirmou que "o Brasil precisa debater com urgência uma reforma política e do Judiciário" e é dever dos agentes públicos do país atender a esse desejo da população.

"É chegada a hora da Justiça brasileira recuperar a sua credibilidade. A atividade da magistratura precisa de juízes isentos, éticos e livres de conflito de interesses e projetos de enriquecimento. Com uma Justiça eficaz, poderemos encarar com mais rigor a corrupção, o crime organizado e sonegadores", afirmou Lula.

O presidente voltou a dizer que vai criar o Ministério da Segurança Pública, promessa que Lula tinha condicionado à aprovação da proposta de emenda à Constituição da Segurança Pública, aprovada pelo Senado Federal na terça-feira (3).

Como já havia sido aprovada pela Câmara dos Deputados , a proposta vai à promulgação pelo presidente do Congresso Nacional .

Lula também criticou a atuação das big techs durante as eleições de 2026, que classificou como tentativa de interferência. O presidente afirmou que o processo vem acontecendo também em outros países.

"As chamadas big techs tentaram interferir no processo eleitoral brasileiro, dando milhões de visualizações a conteúdos com desinformação e fake news. Mas, com a participação popular, a verdade venceu a mentira", afirmou.

Reeleito para um quarto mandato, Lula chega ao período pós-eleitoral com o desafio de montar uma nova equipe, negociar com um Congresso Nacional mais à direita e conciliar as promessas apresentadas durante a campanha com as restrições das contas públicas.

O governo começa o novo período sob cobrança principalmente nas áreas de segurança pública, saúde e economia.

No primeiro discurso após a vitória, Lula afirmou que pretende governar para todo o país e indicou como prioridades temas como segurança pública, educação, saúde, regulação das plataformas digitais e a relação com o Congresso.

Mesmo se tratando de uma reeleição, a direção do PT avalia que será necessário fazer uma transição entre o terceiro e o quarto mandatos. O presidente do partido, Edinho Silva, afirmou que Lula deverá conversar com as legendas sobre a composição do novo governo depois da COP31.

Segundo Edinho Silva, neste momento Lula está concentrado em concluir o atual mandato e organizar com os presidentes da Câmara dos Deputados , Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), e do Senado Federal , Davi Alcolumbre (União-AP), as propostas que ainda precisam passar pelo Congresso.

Entre as mudanças já previstas está a criação de um Ministério da Segurança Pública, proposta apresentada durante a campanha.

Congresso será um dos principais desafios

A composição do Congresso é um dos principais obstáculos políticos para o quarto mandato. O PL, partido do candidato derrotado, senador Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ), terá 121 deputados e 29 senadores a partir de 2027.

Além disso, PP, União Brasil, Republicanos, Podemos e Novo apoiaram Flávio Bolsonaro no segundo turno. Juntos, esses cinco partidos elegeram 245 deputados e 51 senadores.

A base formada por PT e partidos aliados é menor. O cenário obrigará o Palácio do Planalto a buscar novamente votos de partidos do centro e do Centrão para formar maioria nas duas Casas. Lula reconheceu esse cenário no discurso após a eleição, mas afirmou que pretende negociar com o Congresso escolhido pelas urnas.

"Eu não escolhi o Congresso, foi o povo que escolheu e é com ele que eu vou votar, vou trabalhar e vou aprovar as coisas", afirmou.

Presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) durante 1ª Reunião do Conselho Nacional para Industrialização de Minerais Críticos e Estratégicos (CIMCE), no Palácio do Planalto. — Foto: Ricardo Stuckert

articles.title: Alaska governor gives vote count update in ‘very close’ Senate race
articles.summary: Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) provided an update on the Last Frontier’s closely watched Senate race as vote counting continues. “It’s very close,” the Alaska...
articles.body:
Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) provided an update on the Last Frontier's closely watched Senate race as vote counting continues.

"It's very close," the Alaska Republican said in an interview with John Catsimatidis on WABC radio, giving an update on what lies ahead in the process.

He said that there is a "big batch" of votes coming in next week on Nov. 13, followed by a "smaller batch" on Nov. 15. The final count will happen on Nov. 25.

The batch next week "will really determine who's going to have the lead there because, right now … candidate Peltola is up by just I think a couple of hundred votes," said Dunleavy, who was term-limited and could not seek reelection this year. The gubernatorial race to replace him remains uncalled.

"If nobody reaches 50 percent, that's when they go through the ranking process in which the other candidates, the ones that have the least votes, they fall off and their votes are redistributed in the manner by which people rank them," the governor added.

"We're still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes and we are in the midst of investigations to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or a misrepresentation of individuals' intent on how they want their candidacy to be placed on the ballot," Dunleavy said.

Alaska and Mississippi are the two states with remaining uncalled Senate contests.

The Senate race in Alaska between Democrat Mary Peltola and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), was dragged into controversy in the weeks leading up to the midterm election.

The Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block certification of the state's election, claiming the presence of a candidate with the same name as the incumbent could give Peltola an unfair advantage. Days before the election, the New York Times reported that the Democrat's campaign was directly involved in recruiting a man named Daniel J. Sullivan in an effort to dilute votes. Peltola has repeatedly denied the allegations.

Following the Times report, Dunleavy ordered an investigation into whether Peltola's campaign violated state law, and the House Oversight Committee launched its own probe into the alleged scheme.

The race has been neck-and-neck with Peltola taking a slight lead over the incumbent with a little over 48 percent of the votes, according to Decision Desk HQ. Sullivan, on the other hand, has secured 47.9 percent of votes with 70 percent of the expected votes counted.

articles.title: MAGA voters reveal who they want to see lead GOP in 2028
articles.summary: MAGA voters at a Trump rally name JD Vance and Marco Rubio as early 2028 presidential election favorites after Democrats swept the midterms.
articles.body:
With Democrats taking control of Congress in the midterm elections, MAGA voters are already sizing up potential successors to President Donald Trump in 2028 — with Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio repeatedly emerging as favorites among those interviewed by Fox News Digital.

"I like [Rubio]," one American told Fox News Digital. "I like that he's no-nonsense, similar to Trump."

"Well, I like JD Vance obviously," another said. "I like Marco Rubio. There's some other ones, too, that are maybe not so much mainstream that are coming up that I like too."

"JD is great too, but Rubio has a little more experience," one said. "He's articulate, he's well-spoken. He's got good ideas. I just really like him."

Fox News Digital spoke with Americans attending a Trump rally in Port Huron, Michigan, as one of Trump's final stops before Tuesday's midterms that ended in a stunning blue wave. Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran , Americans voted to oust Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate.

With Democrats looking to rebuke Trump and his allies, Republicans that Fox News Digital spoke with are looking for a presidential candidate to fill in Trump's "footsteps."

"I'm really open to see who can fill Trump's footsteps, not just the next person in line," one told Fox News Digital.

"I wish Trump could run again," another said.

Another brought up the prospect of another presidential run by Gov. Ron DeSantis , R-Fla., who has tried to distance himself from the results of Tuesday's midterms. In a news conference Wednesday, he praised Florida for keeping the state under GOP control — suggesting his governance was a reason Florida Republicans held on.

"I would like to see either JD and Marco, or JD and Gov. DeSantis," one said at the Trump rally. "That's what I would feel comfortable with. "

Beyond Vance, Rubio and DeSantis, other prominent Republicans whose names have surfaced in early 2028 discussions include Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas and Josh Hawley, R-Mo.

No major Republican contender has formally announced a 2028 presidential campaign , though the conclusion of the midterms has brought the party's next presidential nomination into sharper focus.

Despite some that Fox News Digital spoke with expressing a preference for Rubio over Vance, other Trump supporters stopped short of choosing between the two, praising both as potential successors to the president.

"I like JD Vance, and I like Marco Rubio," one said. "I think those are two very outstanding candidates that will continue to make America great again."

articles.title: Leading Dem on midterms aftermath: "We're still in the fight of our lives"
articles.summary: The midterms marked one of the biggest rebukes of the Republican Party since Watergate. What is the fallout from this year's elections, and how are Democrats...
articles.body:
There were echoes of history in this year's midterm election, one of the biggest rebukes of Republicans since 1974, when Watergate, inflation and unemployment dominated the campaign. That year, Democrats won 291 seats in the House of Representatives (flipping 49 GOP-held seats), and picked up four Senate seats.

Following last Tuesday's elections, Democrats now have robust majorities in both houses of Congress . Florida's Republican Governor Rick DeSantis called it "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans."

There were also stunning upsets in red states, including Kansas , South Carolina and Texas . It was, Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz said, "a Watergate-level repudiation."

Former Maryland Gov. Larry Hogan, a Republican, says his party is at a crossroads. He says the dynamic of many Republicans in the Trump Era being fearful of getting too far away from the president has changed. "Oh, I think it changed on Tuesday," he said, calling this year's midterms "the most disastrous election for Republicans ever."

He added that, of Republicans still in office who don't want to fight Mr. Trump directly, "Like the Cowardly Lion, they'll find that they actually had courage all along."

Hogan was asked what it would take for voters to trust the GOP again: "They didn't like the status quo, and they threw out all the Republicans," he replied. "The Democrats are now in charge. They don't have the White House, but they do have both houses of Congress. And so, now they have to actually deliver on their promises. It's going to be really interesting to see what both parties do. My party has to do a little bit of soul-searching about where do we go from here."

More than a little bit? "A lot!" Hogan laughed.

"I liken it to the Battle of Gettysburg"

President Trump told "Sunday Morning" on Election Day that he will push back hard against Democrats , and on Friday he named the confrontational Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

Democrats, led by New York's Hakeem Jeffries (soon to be the first-ever Black Speaker of the House), are ramping up investigations.

Maryland Congressman Jamie Raskin, set to chair the powerful House Judiciary Committee, says Democrats are going to hold President Trump accountable through the rule of law.

He also does not think Congress should focus on the economy at the expense of investigations: "It's not an either/or proposition," Raskin said. "Take, for example, the French Revolution. Remember when Marie Antoinette said, 'Let them eat cake'? Now, is that a problem of accountability and tyranny, a corrupt government? Or is it a problem of affordability and standard of living? It's both! Authoritarianism and tyranny are extremely expensive for the people.

"And it's the exact same thing when you go down the line with Donald Trump," Raskin said. "So, are we going to go after the corruption? Yeah, you're damn right. And are we going to go after affordability and making people's lives easier? Yeah, you're damn right. We're going to do both of them."

Raskin also believes that, post-elections, bipartisanship is possible. "Sure," he said. "I saw JD Vance make a speech the other day. He's rapidly backpedaling and trying to dissociate himself from the Iran War. Let's work in a bipartisan way to try to extricate ourselves from the mess they got us into. Same thing with the tariffs, right? They're all backpedaling from the tariffs."

But Raskin says, following his party's major wins last Tuesday, Democrats have no illusions about the road ahead: "It was a huge victory, but I liken it to the Battle of Gettysburg, which was a turning point in the Civil War, but it wasn't the end of it," he said. "There were a lot more battles to come. And Donald Trump still has two years in office, at least on paper. This struggle is not over by a long shot. We're still in the fight of our lives."

Story produced by Mary Raffalli. Editor: Ed Givnish.

articles.title: Democrats won big on Election Day. But can they agree on AI?
articles.summary: Democrats campaigned on concerns about AI and data centers, but competing priorities and opposition from the Trump administration could complicate efforts to...
articles.body:
Democrats across the country who swept into power amid growing voter skepticism about AI and data centers are now reckoning with knotty discussions about how to tackle AI regulation and which technological impacts deserve their attention first, according to AI experts, strategists and legislators themselves.

Dusted with confetti and batting away Election Day balloons, midterm victors touched on everything from data centers — Sen.-elect Chris Pappas of New Hampshire railed against the facilities that "harm our communities and our well-being" — to healthcare, as Sen.-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota committed to restricting the use of AI systems in insurance decisions.

The renewed calls for AI regulation are at odds with President Donald Trump's insistence that Congress must limit AI-focused regulation or risk hampering American AI innovation. Trump has repeatedly referred to AI as a "golden goose" and data centers as sound economic investments.

It is unclear whether Tuesday's results could create a new opening for meaningful bipartisan AI legislation — with representatives mindful of voters' AI hawkishness — or instead result in messy infighting within the Democratic Party, Congress and Washington.

"Every Democrat in the House I'm speaking to wants to see AI regulation," said incoming representative Scott Wiener, who pioneered California's state-level regulation about AI and will represent San Francisco. "There may be different ideas about what that should be, but I think there's broad support to take action."

Some Democrats, like Ohio's Sherrod Brown, have focused their attention on data centers, often viewed as the physical manifestation of nebulous AI worries and which have stressed electrical grids and water supplies in some areas. "I do not work for data centers," he said Tuesday night in a state that has one of the highest concentrations of the facilities in the country.

Others, like re-elected Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia, have also highlighted the technology's catastrophic risks. "The titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they're creating risks human extinction," he said in his victory speech.

Polls and pundits agree that AI played a significant role in the election. "Six months ago, if you had told me that 56% of voters would have left their polling places stating that concerns about AI were crucial or important to their vote, I would have looked at you like you had 10 heads," said Sacha Haworth, founder and CEO of the Tech Oversight Project , a Washington, D.C.-based watchdog and advocacy group.

Yet some AI experts predict that the variety of Democrats' AI priorities could lead to fractured policy approaches and watered-down legislation, while other party leaders on AI predicted a more cooperative result.

"I think the Democrats are going to have a hard time wrangling their own perspectives on this," said Samuel Hammond, director of AI policy at the Foundation for American Innovation, a right-leaning Washington, D.C., think tank. He highlighted the distance between proposals like the one championed by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., to ban artificial superintelligence — referring to systems smarter than humans at all cognitive tasks — and more prosaic efforts to update permitting guidelines to build power plants and other AI-related infrastructure.

Alex Bores, a New York Assembly member who authored one of the country's most substantial pieces of AI legislation — the RAISE Act — disagreed. He framed candidates' differing priorities as an asset that will allow Congress to tackle many critical AI policy initiatives simultaneously.

Multiple policy approaches are "good and healthy as long as we're working together to ensure that we are protecting the American people from the many different ways that this technology could harm people," he said. "There is so much that we have to do in AI, foundational to who gets to decide what we're building."

Bores also said that pro-AI funding had proved toxic to some candidates, pointing to significant losses for candidates supported by pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future. The organization also spent heavily against Bores in his own primary campaign for Congress earlier this year, which he narrowly lost.

AI experts also predicted that Washington's previous AI proposals would likely be significantly reimagined under the new political order.

Before the election, a bipartisan bill co-sponsored by Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., called the FRONTIER Act had worked its way through Washington as one of the most likely pieces of legislation to pass.

The bill would require increased independent testing and oversight of the most advanced AI systems and mandate that leading AI companies create and publish safety-focused plans. However, Obernolte has faced an unusually competitive re-election battle. As of Sunday morning, his race had not been decided, according to NBC News.

Congress has not passed a significant AI law in recent years, in large part because Trump has opposed regulation. The president and his allies, many of whom hail from Silicon Valley's tech circles, have insisted that legislation will stifle America's economy and the AI industry.

"The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor," Trump wrote in a Truth Social post in late August.

The Trump administration has repeatedly endorsed federal bills that would pre-empt, or override, state-level legislation. David Sacks, the former White House AI czar and current chair of the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, has said that state laws would lead to a harmful "patchwork" of legislation.

Yet Tuesday's results point to increasing bipartisan interest in passing meaningful AI legislation, according to the Foundation for American Innovation's Hammond. "AI is not nearly as left-right polarized as most other issues," he said.

"Post-midterms, I think Republicans will feel less pressure from tech money and have, at least in the short run, greater degrees of freedom to express their parallel concerns about AI," he added.

articles.title: Sanders warns Democrats about spending too much time investigating Trump
articles.summary: “We've got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives,” Sen. Bernie Sanders said.
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders on Sunday applauded the Democrats' midterm victories but warned the incoming majority against spending too much time investigating President Donald Trump.

In an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press," the Vermont progressive said holding the Trump administration "accountable" is important — but addressing affordability must take priority.

"We cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump," Sanders said. "We've got to stand up for working-class families, make a real difference in their lives."

Democrats ran on a message of affordability ahead of the midterms, knocking the Trump administration for sky-high gas and grocery prices, the cost of living and rising healthcare costs. But they also vowed to investigate administration officials; incoming House Oversight Committee leader Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Sunday warned that Democrats could investigate everything from pardons Trump made earlier in his second term to Trump allies including Elon Musk and the president's newly appointed chief of staff Stephen Miller.

Still, Sanders on Sunday said the election was about more than just Americans wanting to tackle the Trump administration's "corruption and illegal, unconstitutional actions."

"What I think this election was about, is the American people not only expressing disgust with Trump and his policies, but are demanding real change, no more tinkering around the edges," said Sanders. "And what the American people are saying: Look, we are working long hours. We're worried about our kids. We can't afford healthcare. We can't afford housing."

But Sanders, who serves on the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (HELP) , also told CNN's "State of the Union" that he would be "open" to a proposal by Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) to impeach Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr.

"At the very least, I think, he is the most dangerous secretary of the HHS in history and he needs to be held accountable," said Sanders. "We're going to bring him before the committee, that's for sure, and ask him some tough questions that have not been asked of him previously."

And though Sanders accused Trump of being "erratic," he added that the president is "a good politician" that Democrats may be able to work with.

"I think, when Trump looks out in the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage," said Sanders. "He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does: guaranteeing healthcare to all people."

articles.title: Hamilton: Many people in Kansas view Schumer as ‘polarizing’
articles.summary: Adam Hamilton, the newly elected Democratic Kansas senator, said Sunday that many people in Kansas view Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as “polarizing.” NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked Hamilton during his interview Sunday on “Meet the Press” why the top Senate Democrat, whom Hamilton has been critical of before, is not the right leader…
articles.body:
Adam Hamilton, the newly elected Democratic Kansas senator, said Sunday that many people in Kansas view Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as “polarizing.”

NBC News’s Kristen Welker asked Hamilton during his interview Sunday on “Meet the Press” why the top Senate Democrat, whom Hamilton has been critical of before, is not the right leader for the party.

“I mean no disrespect for Chuck Schumer,” Hamilton told Welker. “And I’ve told him that as well. But I think, at least where I live in Kansas, he is kind of a polarizing figure.”

Hamilton noted that his opponent on the campaign trail, incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall (R), “mentioned Chuck Schumer far more than he ever mentioned me. It was, like, 17 or 18 times.” He said that Kansans “perceive him [Schumer] to be further to the left, and somebody who’s a divisive figure.”

“What I’d be looking for is a leader who can lead from the center,” the Kansas Democrat continued. “Somebody who can bring Republicans and Democrats together, somebody who can bring the various factions in the Democratic Party together. Somebody with fresh ideas.”

He repeated that he meant no disrespect to Schumer but said “it feels like … it is a time for fresh, new ideas, and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us.”

When asked who he would pick to be Schumer’s successor, Hamilton said, “I’ll tell you, I’ve been a pastor for 38 years. I know probably 10 senators personally, and even those I only know from brief conversations.”

“So, you know, I’m not at a place where I can tell you, ‘This is my short list,’” he explained. “There are a handful of people that I think are probably –– you know, lead more from the center. But I don’t know enough yet to be able to say, ‘These are the people I would endorse.’”

Schumer, though he faces some dissent from members of his own party, has enough votes to become Senate majority leader next month. He needs only a majority of the Democratic caucus, which is projected to have at least 54 members and possibly as many as 56 in January.

Other newly elected Democratic senators who have said they would not back Schumer as Senate majority leader include Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed, Maine’s Troy Jackson and Minnesota’s Peggy Flanagan.

The New York Democrat told reporters Wednesday that he was not the “issue” and that he will be reelected to lead Democrats in the Senate.

“But the issue is focusing on the American people and what they want,” Schumer said.

Others outside of the Senate disapprove of Schumer returning to power.

The progressive group Indivisible called for Democrats to replace Schumer, saying that Americans “did not elect Democrats by historic margins just to bend the knee and go back to business as usual.”

Comedian Jon Stewart similarly said Schumer “does not understand the urgency of the moment and what the future demands.”

“Someone has to meet this moment, and they have got to show — and this moment is not, ‘Oh, we get to impeach everybody,’ like f— that,” Stewart said Thursday on “ The Weekly Show ” podcast. “Like, you have an opportunity to actually govern. Do it. Take it.”

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Sunday said Democrats will need to hold President Trump accountable when they take over control of Congress starting in January but added that they “cannot spend all of our time” just investigating the president.

“Do we want to hold the Trump administration accountable for their corruption, for their illegal, unconstitutional actions? Absolutely,” Sanders told NBC News’s Kristen Welker during his appearance on “Meet the Press.”

But Sanders said that with a slew of issues that Senate Democrats should handle, “we cannot spend all of our time investigating Trump.”

“We ought to stand up for working class families, make a real difference in their lives,” he said.

Sanders called for passing single-payer healthcare — or “Medicare for All” — within the first year of Democratic control in Congress and said that he thinks Trump “is mentally unbalanced, erratic, but he’s not stupid and he’s a good politician,” and could therefore work with Democrats to make meaningful changes.

“He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does, guaranteeing healthcare to people,” the Vermont Independent said.

Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday dodged questions on CNN’s “State of the Union” about Democrats’ calls to investigate the president, his family and members of his Cabinet. He pointed to rhetoric and alleged threats to donors and individuals who are conservative and “might want to work for conservative institutions or for a conservative government or for President Trump.”

“You are allowed to be critical of President Trump, of me, of this administration. But when the threats become so vile and so dangerous that you are telling people in college that they better be careful if they want to work in the Trump administration, because somebody will come after them at some point. You have to draw the line,” Blanche added.

Democrats have said they will flex their investigative muscles after their historic wins this week — with Democratic Rep. Robert Garcia (Calif.), who will soon chair the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, calling on the administration to “Lawyer up.”

“We’re going to bring accountability to those who have visited unprecedented corruption on this country,” Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), set to be the next House Speaker, said Tuesday. “Because if you have people in high office who are so focused on enriching themselves, their family members, their friends or their donors, then they’re not focused on making life better for the American people. But House Democrats will put the American people first.”

But the cost of living was a leading issue going into the midterms, with many Americans saying they did not approve of Trump’s handling of the economy and inflation.

The launch of the Iran war led to soaring fuel prices, with gas costing $1 more a gallon than the national average last year, according to AAA . Data from the travel agency showed that the average price for gas costs $4.02 as of Sunday.

articles.title: Trump vows comeback as bitter showdown with Congress looms
articles.summary: Donald Trump vowed a political comeback Sunday as the major parties clashed over Democrat threats to prosecute top administration officials after the preside...
articles.body:
Donald Trump vowed a political comeback Sunday as the major parties clashed over Democrat threats to prosecute top administration officials after the president's Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections.

The devastating results in last Tuesday's vote leave Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the remaining two-year 'lame duck' period of his White House tenure, while opening the door to multiple investigations by the Democrat-controlled Congress of the president, his family and senior members of his administration.

On political talk shows Sunday, incoming congressional leaders from the Democratic Party promised to hold Trump and his aides to account, while the president's top law officer resolved to defend them and Trump dug in his heels on social media.

"America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election," Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the stock market that had grown during his tenure took a loss after the vote.

"But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!"

On Friday, a defiant Trump appointed hardline advisor Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback -- even though many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have reflected on why they had lost so badly at the ballot box.

Miller was architect of Trump's tough immigration policy that analysts have identified as a contributing factor to the unpopularity of Republicans.

Amid Democrat threats for administration officials to "lawyer up," Trump said Saturday he was ordering the Justice Department to examine Democratic threats to impeach members of his administration, likening it to "extortion."

That stance stoked a war of words between top Republicans and Democrats on the Sunday talk shows.

Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump and now head of the Justice Department, vowed to actively defend Trump and senior members of his administration.

"You have members of Congress who, after Tuesday, have done nothing but threaten everything that's happening in this administration," Blanche told CNN, citing impeachment threats against Miller after his appointment.

"If they try to come after Stephen Miller...instead of actually just conducting oversight and leading, of course the Department of Justice will be there to defend him."

Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, took aim at Blanche, saying one role of Congress under the US constitution is to hold the executive branch to account.

"All he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump's cabinet and administration officials. That is not his job," Garcia told CNN, vowing to stop corruption and investigate "those that are committing crimes against the American public."

"They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated," added Garcia.

With control of committees in both chambers of Congress, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny.

Likely subjects include the Trump family's business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war.

Hakeem Jeffries, set to become speaker of the new Democrat-controlled House of Representatives, said he would support an effort to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of the war on Iran that began in February.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC, when asked about a Republican lawmaker's reported plan to introduce an impeachment motion as early as Monday.

"The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go."

During his first presidency, Trump himself was impeached by the House twice, but on both occasions he was acquitted by the Senate.

articles.title: El-Sayed says he is ‘happy’ to work with Trump on Medicare for all, other priorities
articles.summary: “If he wants to pass Trumpcare for all … I’m game,” said Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed.
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday opened the door to potentially working with President Donald Trump to pass legislation securing nationwide affordable healthcare.

In an interview with ABC's "This Week," the progressive from Michigan called Trump an "unserious fool" but said he would be "happy" to sit down with the president to discuss how best to serve Michiganders.

"Look, I've never met the man. I am — he is the president of the United States. I am the U.S. senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him like I'll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on: to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for All," El-Sayed said. "I've said this, if he wants to pass Trump Care for All, which will guarantee health care to everyone and put his name on it like he's putting his name on everything, I'm game. Let's see if he wants to do that."

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Trump was vociferous in his criticism of El-Sayed throughout the campaign season, lambasting El-Sayed for his progressive policies and repeatedly mocking his name.

Trump had supported former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in the bitter Michigan race. El-Sayed on Sunday said he is not aware of any attempts at communication from Rogers.

"I think he has a flight to catch to Florida," El-Sayed quipped. Though born and raised in Michigan, Rogers moved to Florida with his wife after leaving Congress in 2015. (Rogers' campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

Despite his apparent openness to meet with Trump, El-Sayed criticized the president for appointing Stephen Miller to be the White House's new chief of staff — evidence, El-Sayed argued, of Trump's lack of seriousness when Americans are demanding affordability and accountability.

"So, look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," he said. "He is the president of the United States, but he wants to continue to fool he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House. And he gets to choose where he goes next."

articles.title: Trump set to lurch further right, claiming US took ‘giant step back’ in elections
articles.summary: Trump poised to double down on immigration crackdown and refuse concessions to new Democratic majority in Congress
articles.body:
Donald Trump set the stage for his administration to lurch further to the right this weekend, claiming the US had taken a "giant step back" by widely rejecting his party.

The US president's hardline aide, Stephen Miller, will begin as White House chief of staff on Monday. He will also meet with Dana White, CEO and president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, after offering him the job of press secretary .

"America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election," Trump claimed in a post on his Truth Social platform on Sunday morning, citing the sharp sell-off in global markets, fueled a rout of US tech stocks. "But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!"

Despite Republicans losing control of both chambers of US Congress in Tuesday's decisive US midterm elections, and voters across the country expressing frustration with key pillars of Trump's controversial agenda, from the Iran war to sweeping tariffs, the administration appears set to press ahead.

Miller's promotion has stoked expectations that Trump is poised to double down on an aggressive immigration crackdown, stoke cultural war battles, and refuse concessions to the new Democratic majority in Congress. The move "signals the administration is going to ⁠have a fighting-from-a-bunker approach the last two years", Dan Eberhart, a Trump donor and energy executive, told Reuters.

Trump abruptly announced on Saturday that he had offered White, whom he described as "a violent Fighter and Warrior", the role of White House press secretary, which has been largely vacant since Karoline Leavitt departed the administration this summer . Leavitt initial replacement, Katie Zacharia, lasted five days in the job .

"Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other," said Trump. "Dana, please take the job!"

After Trump also threatened Democrats planning to conduct oversight of his administration and family, announcing he had ordered the US Department of Justice to "look into" them, attorney general Todd Blanche told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday that " there could be " investigations. Republicans have faced "dangerous" threats, Blanche claimed, without specifying what crimes he believed had been committed. "You have to draw the line."

Democrats have made clear that Miller and Elon Musk, the world's richest man and a close Trump ally, are likely to be targets of congressional investigations once the party retakes control of Congress in January.

Congressman Robert Garcia, a Democrat from California, who is set to chair the powerful oversight committee in the House of Representatives next year, said on Sunday that investigations are set to explore Musk's involvement in the Department of Government Efficiency's mass firing of federal workers last year, and Miller's role in Trump's immigration crackdown. "I think there's a lot ⁠of interest – not just from our committee, but from committees across the Congress – to speak to Mr Musk," Garcia told CNN.

Representative Jamie Raskin, poised to become the chair of the House judiciary committee, has also requested information on the business dealings of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr.

With 33 of 35 Senate races called, the Democrats had won 54 seats to the Republicans' 44. Votes are still being counted in Alaska, which had long been seen as a key battleground, and Mississippi, a previous Republican stronghold which remains too close to call.

Congressman James Comer, a Republican from Kentucky who currently heads the House oversight committee before his party cedes control to Democrats, told Fox News that the committee is going to dedicate the last two months of this congress investigating Alaska over the controversy surrounding its Senate race.

Trump has already threatened Democratic candidate Mary Peltola with criminal prosecution over reports that her campaign was linked to the recruitment of a second "Dan Sullivan" in Alaska's Senate race, with the same name as the Republican candidate.

Democrats meanwhile embarked on a victory lap this weekend, celebrating their historic wins on Tuesday. Democratic candidates won after running on policies that would "change working peoples' lives", New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani told Fox News on Sunday.

"We are seeing a moment in time where working class Americans have made very clear that they are tired of waiting," said Mamdani. "They are tired of being told, again and again, that there is less for them to make ends meet, while we see the world's first trillionaire emerge in Elon Musk."

But there has been friction within the party regarding the incoming congressional leadership, with Chuck Schumer set to become the next majority leader in the US Senate Hakeem Jeffries widely expected to become House speaker.

Senator-elect Adam Hamilton of Kansas – the first Democrat the state has sent to the US Senate in almost a century – told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday the Schumer is a "kind of polarizing figure" adding: "It feels like it is a time for fresh and new ideas, and somebody who can unite us instead of dividing us."

During a Saturday Night Live skit this weekend, a member of the cast impersonated Trump attacking James Talarico, the Democrat who ran for US Senate in Texas, and called him "Talafreako" – only for Talarico himself to walk out on stage.

"That's senator Talafreako," he said, to loud cheers, after becoming the first Democrat to win statewide office in Texas since 1994 .

articles.title: AI nearly had US troops attack a Chinese ship. Nobody could check its work.
articles.summary: The lack of independent oversight and verifiable records in artificial intelligence deployment poses significant risks to national security, finance and healthcare, necessitating a solution similar to aviation’s flight recorders.
articles.body:
In the middle of the war with Iran this spring, a U.S. aircraft was airborne and armed personnel were preparing to board a Chinese ship in the Middle East. A chatbot had reviewed intelligence on the ship’s cargo manifest and concluded it was carrying components for a nuclear weapons program.

An analyst had used AI to reach that conclusion. He then used AI again to write it up as a formal intelligence report, which circulated across the military before officials looked closer and called the operation off.

Models get things wrong all the time, so the error itself isn’t what’s worrying. What’s worrying is how close it came to holding. The report gave nobody a way to check how it reached its conclusion. That same gap exists almost everywhere AI is being deployed, from military intelligence to bank lending to hospital care. Closing it is less a matter of new rules than of keeping records that let someone check an AI system’s work.

On Sept. 18, CNN broke the story , citing four sources, days before President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping met in Washington with AI on the agenda. The U.S. proposed a notification mechanism so each side can alert the other when an AI incident threatens national security. Helen Toner, who leads Georgetown’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology, has gone further proposing a National Transportation Safety Board for AI — a body with the technical expertise to receive and investigate serious AI incidents.

Both proposals make sense, but investigators can only examine an incident if they can reproduce it. The National Transportation Safety Board works because every plane carries a flight recorder, and investigators read the data rather than reconstructing a crash from memory. AI has nothing like that. Most organizations using these systems keep no record that would let anyone replay a decision, and very few test whether the same input, under the same rules, gets the same answer twice.

This week, my team published a case where that test failed. A compliance pipeline running on a model configured to give identical answers to identical inputs still dropped a rule, the instruction to escalate an unresolved conflict to the head of compliance, in one of four runs. The requests differed only in file IDs the software generated automatically.

Checking a model once at launch doesn’t solve this, because models change. When DeepSeek moved its latest model from preview to official release this summer, my team re-ran an audit we published weeks earlier. Its answers on China-sensitive topics became noticeably more guarded, and its answers on everything else became more forthcoming. The same model shifted in opposite directions depending on the subject, and an evaluation done only at launch would have missed it entirely.

AI systems can also find ways around the tests we give them. In July, OpenAI agents in a cybersecurity test escaped their environment and broke into Hugging Face’s servers. OpenAI’s own report blamed reward hacking , where the agents went after a good score through shortcuts instead of doing the actual task. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) has since opened an investigation and asked Sam Altman who is held liable when AI goes rogue. Every company deploying AI should be asking itself the same question.

In most cases, the answer is the company using it. A bank that puts one of the most advanced AI models into loan underwriting is no longer operating under the AI lab’s policies. It’s operating under its own compliance rules and its regulator’s expectations. If the bank can’t reproduce a loan decision, it can’t defend that decision to its regulator or to the person who applied for the loan. Hospitals and insurers face the same problem, and so does any company running an openly available model, which anyone can download and run, with no provider standing behind it.

On Sept. 29 , leaders of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI and Nvidia signed a White House accord committing to independent outside evaluators. On Oct. 3, the White House formed a task force, led by the director of national intelligence, with 120 days to recommend the federal government’s role. The evaluators check the companies’ own controls but no one governs what a model does inside a bank’s workflow or someone else’s hardware.

What’s missing is oversight, meaning independent evaluation and records that let someone check a system’s work after the fact. Human reviewers can’t do that at scale. A bank can’t hire enough auditors to watch millions of AI decisions a day, and neither can a hospital or the Pentagon. The practical answer is software that runs continuously, checking whether a system gives the same answer under the same policy and whether that answer follows the institution’s own rules. Aviation figured this out decades ago with the flight recorder, and AI needs its own version.

This is also one of the few parts of the AI debate where the U.S. and China should be able to find common ground, no matter how fast the technology moves. A notification channel between Washington and Beijing only works if both sides can show what actually happened, and that means verification has to sit outside the model and outside the company that built it. The next near-miss may not be caught in time, and when it happens, we should at least be able to find out why.

Cyril Gorlla is CEO of CTGT , an applied interpretability lab in San Francisco, and convenes the American Society for AI’s working group on post-deployment verification.

articles.body:
Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) on Sunday decried President Trump’s promotion of Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff.

“I come from the business world, just like President Trump does. And you know what? If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” Stutzman told CNN’s Manu Raju on “Inside Politics,” referencing the recent midterm elections. “You don’t promote those who are — who were in charge of what was supposed to be delivered.”

“I think that the decision to elect Stephen Miller is a mistake. He’s not liked out here in the Midwest by people, they don’t like his tone,” he added.

On Friday, Trump announced that chief of staff Susie Wiles was leaving the White House and Miller, a longtime adviser to the president, would take her place.

Miller’s promotion followed Republicans getting bombarded with defeats in the midterms, with the House and Senate going to Democrats.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who will most likely become House Speaker next year, on Friday called Miller “a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist who has American blood on his hands.”

“His presence in government should be eradicated like a malignant tumor. Fire him today,” Jeffries continued in a post on the social platform X.

When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement that Miller “has been a key player in delivering on President Trump’s America First agenda since day one.”

Sanders said he believes Trump is “mentally unbalanced, erratic, but…
articles.body:
Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) on Sunday said he’s “not worried” about Stephen Miller becoming President Trump’s new White House chief of staff.

“Meet the Press” host Kristen Welker pointed out Sanders’s history of criticizing Miller and asked if he could see himself working with him. Sanders said he believes Trump is “mentally unbalanced, erratic, but he’s not stupid and he’s a good politician.”

“And I think when Trump looks out on the world and he sees millions of people working for starvation wages, he might not be unsympathetic to raising the minimum wage to a living wage,” Sanders continued. “He would love, I think, to take credit for doing what every other major country does, guaranteeing healthcare to all people.”

Sanders added, “So I’m not worried about Miller. Do I think we can work with Trump? Maybe. By no means guaranteeing it, but it is certainly worth the effort.”

After Democrats made sweeping gains in the 2026 midterm elections, many have also called for investigating and executing oversight on the Trump administration.

Sanders urged his Democratic colleagues who he generally caucuses with to not “spend all of our time investigating Trump.”

“We ought to stand up for working class families, make a real difference in their lives,” he said.

Miller was tapped to replace Susie Wiles as the White House chief of staff following the Republican defeat during the midterms. A longtime ally to Trump and champion of his rhetoric, Miller pledged “my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success and the success of this country” in remarks on Friday.

The Vermont senator has long criticized Miller’s right-wing views on immigration and other issues. Sanders dismissed Vice President Vance’s claim that the democratic socialist and Miller sounded as though they were aligned on the issue of closing the U.S.-Mexico border as it related to American workers during an interview with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins last month.

He said that it was Republican “mythology” that any Democrats campaigned on opening the southern border and explained that the country should appreciate “the hard work” of migrants already in the country and move toward “comprehensive immigration reform and a path for citizenship.”

“So you don’t think you sound like Stephen Miller?” Collins asked.

“No,” Sanders said with a chuckle. “Please, no.”

He had also clapped back at Miller’s claim that the U.S. runs and controls Venezuela following the U.S. capture of President Nicolás Maduro in January.

“Well, Mr. Miller gave a very good definition of imperialism,” he told CNN’s Jake Tapper when asked to respond to Miller’s remarks.
