articles.summary: Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy calls ranked-choice voting "very confusing" as Mary Peltola leads Dan Sullivan by just 637 votes in Senate race.
articles.body:
Republican Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy admits his own state's voting system is "very confusing," and warned that the close race between Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola and incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan will not be determined for days, if not weeks.

"It's very close, the numbers," Dunleavy told WABC Radio's "The Cats Roundtable" on Sunday, noting key dates for ballot dumps will be Friday, Nov. 13, and Wednesday, Nov. 18, when "another big batch of votes will come in."

"It's a slow system up here in Alaska," he admitted, acknowledging that "we've got quite an issue up here."

"A big batch of votes will come and that'll really determine, you know, who's going to have the lead."

Peltola, currently with 48.17% support, leads by just 637 votes in Alaska's ranked-choice voting system that has not dropped any new vote tallies for days. Election Day was Tuesday, Nov. 3, and if no candidate gets 50% support as the No. 1 choice by Nov. 25, the results go to rounds of ranked-choice candidates on the second and third choices.

"It is very confusing," Dunleavy said. "That was also on the ballot, to actually repeal that voting scheme that was put in place here just a couple years ago, and so it's confusing, 100%."

"No" votes against repealing ranked-choice voting lead very narrowly at 51.85%. That decision also remains too close to call a week after the polls closed.

"We're still in the process of bringing in votes and counting votes," Dunleavy said. "And we are in the midst of investigations as to determine if there was any wrongdoing, especially anything that might resemble perjury or, you know, a misrepresentation of individual's intent on how they wanted their candidacy to be placed on the ballot."

Dunleavy denounced what he called the " Decoy Dan " scheme that had Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot in an alleged plot to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent.

The governor claimed the other Sullivan even allegedly tried to get on the general election ballot as Daniel S. Sullivan , using the middle initial of the incumbent instead of his own.

"That kind of opened our eyes and we began an investigation back there, the Division of Elections did, to determine if this was a legitimate candidacy, and the Division of Elections at that time found that was not and did not put him on the ballot," Dunleavy said. "Then there was a court case and the Supreme Court in the end ruled against the Division of Elections in Alaska, and they must go on the ballot."

After a New York Times report tied potential knowledge of the "Decoy Dan" scheme on behalf of Peltola's campaign , Dunleavy reopened the investigation of wrongdoing.

"When The New York Times article came out, you know, we already knew a lot of what was happening there, but there was more revelations of that article," he said. "As a result of that, we began another investigation up here in Alaska, and the Department of Justice did the same, so you have this investigation going on right in the middle of an election."

articles.title: Stephen Miller and the DOJ hatching plan to throw journalists in jail over leaks: report
articles.summary: Miller reportedly insisted that it wouldn’t take long for journalists to give up their government sources
articles.body:
Newly appointed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and the Department of Justice have reportedly been considering throwing journalists in jail to get them to reveal their sources when government intel is leaked, according to a report.

Following Susie Wiles' exit as chief of staff, The Atlantic reported that President Donald Trump urged the DOJ to pursue criminal-leak investigations on national security grounds.

There have reportedly been discussions among White House officials about tactics they could use to get journalists to reveal their sources — including arresting them, three people familiar with the subject told the outlet.

Two people described Wiles pushing back against trying to force journalists to divulge their government sources, while Miller was in favor of the move, insisting that it wouldn't take long for journalists to give up their sources, according to the report.

A DOJ spokesperson told The Atlantic : "This is absolutely false," and reiterated that when approached for comment by The Independent.

Meanwhile, a White House spokesperson told The Independent: "Unauthorized leaks of sensitive national security information will NEVER be tolerated. They endanger American lives and threaten our national security. Those responsible must be held accountable."

It is not illegal for journalists to receive — and write about — classified information they have received from a government leaker, even if the source themselves has violated the law by sharing the information.

In 1971, The New York Times published excerpts of a leaked report detailing the U.S. involvement in the Vietnam War, prompting the Nixon administration to try and block the publication of the leaked files. However, the Supreme Court ruled in favor of the newspaper and press freedom.

On Friday, Trump revealed that his longtime aide, Miller, would be replacing Wiles, who Trump was reportedly "furious" with after Republicans lost control of Congress in last week's midterm elections.

A longtime proponent of expansive presidential authority, Miller takes over at a time when the Republican Party's midterm defeat could leave Trump more reliant on executive power to advance his domestic agenda.

Miller, 41, is one of Trump's longest-serving aides and one of only a few who have worked for the president throughout both his first and second terms in office.

However, he is best known for driving Trump's aggressive immigration crackdown, which has been widely unpopular among Americans. Just 36% of respondents to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed early this week approve of Trump's mass deportation agenda, with 54% disapproving.

Still, Trump announced Miller as Wiles' replacement on Friday.

"I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026," he wrote on Truth Social.

"Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!"

articles.title: After the midterms, where does the Republican Party stand?
articles.summary: GOP suffered a loss, but it is hardly a historic one. A party in power has always been held to account in the midterms.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, the United States held midterm elections. Every one of the 435 seats in the US House of Representatives was up for election and 35 of the 100 US Senate seats were on the ballot.

The result of the elections was overwhelmingly in favour of the Democratic Party, or the blue team, as the US media has taken to referring to them. It was a blue wave. A blue tsunami. Democrats flipped at least 40 House seats and seven Senate seats. It was a clear message to Washington that much of the US is unhappy with the direction the country is headed.

Texas had not elected a Democrat in a statewide race for more than 30 years. Democrats dominated in Texas. Kansas hadn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1932. Come the first week of January, there will be one representing it. Susan Collins, the powerful Republican chair of the Senate Committee on Appropriations and the most bipartisan voting Republican in the US Senate had been Maine’s senator for 30 years. She was voted out. The depth and breadth of the Democratic victory stunned many.

The war with Iran clearly had an impact. It wasn’t the conflict itself nearly as much as the economic impact it has had on the average American. Virtually every American uses an automobile and the price of petrol has skyrocketed during the war. The high fuel prices have impacted every other segment of the economy because nearly every product, especially food and grocery items, is delivered using the roadway system, which, of course, means petrol and diesel prices add to their cost.

The Democrats taking control of both the House and the Senate will dramatically change the next two years in Washington. They will restore the oversight functions of Congress and will investigate Trump and his team for countless violations, real or imagined. Congressional priorities will change. Impeachment will be a word that is commonly used again. If a vacancy occurs on the Supreme Court, the president will have a much more difficult time filling it. The impact of the elections is very real.

Losing seats to the opposition party is actually quite common in the midterms. Dozens of House races are still being counted, so the final tally may yet grow, but since World War II there have been at least seven midterm elections with seat losses comparable to or larger than what the Republicans have experienced so far in 2026: 1946, 1958, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2010 and 2018 when President Donald Trump’s party lost about 40 House seats in his first midterm.

The largest midterm loss belongs to President Barack Obama’s party in 2010. The Democrats lost 63 House seats and six seats in the Senate. The Democrats would then lose nine seats in the US Senate in the midterm elections held during Obama’s second term.

The Democrats under President Bill Clinton also took a beating in 1994 when the opposition Republicans gained 54 seats in the House, taking a majority for the first time in a generation, and flipping eight seats in the Senate.

The pundits at the time wondered aloud if it was the end of the Democratic Party. The losses were staggering. Both presidents, however, went on to govern effectively and find ways to work with the opposition. In fact, Clinton worked with the Republican Congress to pass the first balanced budget in memory. In that case, the split in government forced them to work together and produced a benefit to the American people.

None of this is new. President Harry Truman’s Democrats lost 55 House seats and 12 Senate seats in 1946. President Dwight Eisenhower’s Republicans took it on the chin in 1958, losing 48 House seats and 13 Senate seats. Presidents Lyndon Johnson, Gerald Ford and George HW Bush all took big losses. Even Ronald Reagan lost 26 House seats in his first midterm elections.

The point is the American public has always demanded accountability from Washington. No one should be surprised that at a time when only 14 percent of Americans think Congress is doing a good job and the prices for basic necessities are increasing, Americans demand change. They have done it over and over, regardless of the party in power.

The next logical question is where do we go from here? Is Trump’s reign as leader of the GOP over? Has he lost his influence?

There will not be a great deal of time spent trying to decipher what went wrong. Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have already acknowledged the war in Iran and its economic effects are the primary reasons for the loss. This acknowledgement will hasten the healing process within the party, as will the need to push through a number of agenda items together in the remaining weeks the Republicans have control of Congress.

Because the US Constitution limits a president to two terms, any time any president enters his final two years, he is known as a lame duck. His influence, while still enormous simply by the reality of the office, begins to wane. The closer it gets to the end of his final term the less influence he has, particularly on the domestic agenda. Many presidents spend the majority of their time near the end of their term on foreign policy.

As of January 3, Democrats will set the agenda on Capitol Hill. They will control every committee. They will control virtually every vote. Congress controls the purse strings, so their impact is large, but don’t count Trump out yet.

His personality and his outward embrace of even the most difficult conflicts are unique. Whether in business, in election wins and losses, in courtroom clashes or in international affairs, Trump doesn’t back down. Admittedly this sometimes works to his detriment, but it is a trait that will likely serve him well as he battles with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The president has veto authority over any legislation Congress passes. Rather than sign the legislation, he can reject it. If he rejects it, two-thirds of both the House and the Senate must vote to override his veto or else the legislation does not become law.

If Trump feels the Democrats are pushing an agenda too radical or too far left, he will wield the veto pen with great regularity.

Ideally the two sides understand the power each holds, and they will work together, as did a Republican-dominated Congress and Democratic President Clinton. If they do work together, all Americans will benefit. If each side digs in and refuses to compromise, it will be a long, unproductive two years.

Speaking of two years, 2028 is the next presidential election, and the question of who will be the nominee for each party is already being kicked around – and, in particular, how these midterm elections will impact the potential Republican candidates like Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

The stark reality is that two years is an eternity in politics. Anything can happen, despite the Republican defeat on Tuesday. The biggest question is whether the American public will be feeling “Trump fatigue” during the 2028 presidential election season.

If the public has grown weary of team Trump, anyone affiliated with his administration may be tainted goods and face a bigger challenge getting the party’s nomination. Vance, Rubio and others directly tied to him have the greatest name recognition right now, but that may prove to be baggage rather than an advantage.

Outsiders such as a state governor or a past political figure may generate public enthusiasm for a different direction. The list is long. Even Trump has said his party has a deep bench, and it’s true.

Trying to predict the 2028 nominee now, in such a volatile political time and with two years to go, while entertaining, is a fool’s errand.

Some in the media have begun to write the Republican Party’s obituary after Tuesday’s losses. The final numbers are not yet in, and in the Senate, the seven seats already lost exceed the six Obama’s party gave up in 2010.

Still, history shows that parties and presidents have come back from setbacks of this scale before, as Obama and Clinton both did. Trump and the Republicans can do the same.

A version of this piece was first published by Al Jazeera Arabic .

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says he is a ‘hard yes’ on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth
articles.body: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said he is a “hard yes” on supporting impeachment efforts against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which are expected to be brought to a vote this week. Asked in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” whether he would support Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., in his efforts to impeach Hegseth, Jeffries confirmed he supported the push. “I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe.” “Pete Hegseth has got to go,” he added. Jeffries’ support marks a major endorsement of impeachment efforts against Hegseth and signals how other House Democrats could ultimately vote on the measure. The impeachment push also tests how far lawmakers are willing to go to oust the top Pentagon official after voters have given low marks to the administration’s handling of the war in Iran, which factored into midterms. Asked on ABC whether Jeffries believed all other House Democrats would support the impeachment resolution, he said that they would “have that conversation Tuesday morning.” The House is back in session this week, and the impeachment resolution is expected to be filed early this week with a vote to follow. Massie has been a vocal critic of Hegseth and the war in Iran. He previously filed a resolution to impeach Hegseth in September, but Republican leaders canceled planned votes and the House left early, pushing the vote to after the election. NBC News reported last week that President Donald Trump has told allies that he was considering replacing Hegseth. Trump, though, has publicly denied that he is planning to replace the secretary, telling reporters last week that Hegseth was “doing a very good job.” At the same time, Hegseth has forcefully pushed back on Massie’s impeachment plans, referring to the congressman in a social media video last week as a “disgruntled, defeated congressman.” “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said in the video. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.” Massie, though, said in a social media post last week that his “Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress.” Democrats, Massie said, would “have hearings & trials.”

articles.title: Previously unreported votes reverse lead in Georgia state House race, threatening Democrats’ narrow majority
articles.summary: A vote-counting discrepancy in Seminole County has put a Republican incumbent ahead in a state legislative contest, prompting an investigation
articles.body:
A vote-counting discrepancy in Seminole County has put a Republican incumbent ahead in a state legislative contest, prompting an investigation into how 388 votes went unreported on election night.

A closely contested Georgia state House race has taken an unexpected turn after election officials identified 388 previously unreported votes in southwest Georgia, reversing the apparent outcome of a contest that could determine just how much power Democrats hold in the state legislature.

The discrepancy involves Georgia House District 154, not the governor's race or a congressional election.

Republican incumbent Gerald Greene had been trailing Democratic challenger Harry James by just 58 votes following Tuesday's election. But after the additional votes were included in Seminole Country's totals, Greene moved ahead by 262 votes, according to The Atlanta Journal-Constitution .

Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger has launched an investigation into why the votes were not included in the initial results and whether election officials followed required procedures.

"This oversight didn't just affect the numbers — it changed who was leading an election," Raffensperger said. "That is unacceptable, and we intend to find out exactly how it happened."

The discrepancy was uncovered during routine post-election checks when state officials noticed that approximately 388 more voters had checked in at Seminole County polling places than the number of ballots reported as cast.

Although initial reports described the issue as a missing memory card, Seminole County Elections Supervisor Ron Foskey disputed that characterization Saturday, saying all memory cards had been accounted for on election night.

According to Foskey, the county's election management system had not completed the final step necessary to validate and publish results from the last precinct's memory card. Once that step was completed, the updated totals matched the county's ballot scanner records.

The county maintained that its chain-of-custody procedures were followed. State officials are investigating how the reporting error occurred.

The implications extend beyond one legislative district.

Democrats emerged from Tuesday's election poised to control the Georgia House of Representatives for the first time in more than two decades. But the reversal in District 154 could leave the party with just 92 seats in the 180-member chamber, only one more than the 91 needed for a majority.

Another legislative contest remains unresolved. Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas faces Democrat Ethan Wolfe in a Dec. 1 runoff, leaving the chamber's final balance of power unsettled.

The District 154 contest is also significant because Greene, who was first elected as a Democrat in 1982 before switching parties after the 2010 election, is currently the only Republican in Georgia's General Assembly representing a majority-Black district, according to the AJC.

The corrected vote totals have not ended scrutiny of the election. Raffensperger's office is examining what went wrong and what measures may be necessary to prevent similar reporting discrepancies in future elections.

County officials face a Monday deadline to certify their election results.

articles.summary: Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in a Nov. 8 television appearance that the elevation of Stephen Miller to White House Chief of Staff was "irresponsibl...
articles.body:
Democratic House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that his party will not work with Stephen Miller , President Donald Trump 's new chief of staff, during an appearance on ABC's " This Week " Nov. 8.

"There's not going to be any opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents," Jeffries said.

Miller was tapped to replace former chief of staff Susie Wiles on Nov. 6 and will step into the role on Nov. 9.

He is a long-time advisor to Trump, dating back to his first term, and the top architect of the Trump administration's anti-immigration crackdown.

Jeffries, who is likely to be the next Speaker of the House when Democrats assume the majority in January, called the move "an awful choice" and "irresponsible." He previously called Miller a "dangerous xenophobe" and a "reckless extremist" when the change was announced.

"(Miller) has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good," Jeffries said on "This Week." "He clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance and the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated."

He added that Democrats will have a "firewall" in Congress against the Trump administration following the Nov. 3 midterms.

Jeffries says Hegseth impeachment has Democratic support

Jeffries said during the appearance on "This Week" that an impeachment vote against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegesth could come as early as this week and would have "incredibly strong" Democratic support. He added that he is a "hard yes" on the resolution introduced by outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky.

"The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said. "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Candidates make history in race, gender and faith in 2026

In eight impeachment articles , Massie accused Hegseth of conducting the war on Iran without congressional authorization, seizing Venezuela's President Nicolás Maduro without constitutional authority and killing suspected drug traffickers in the Caribbean without judicial authorization.

Hegseth has vowed to fight the charges and refused calls to resign following the GOP's wipeout in the midterms attributed in-part to the ongoing war.

The lame-duck Republican majority can kill the impeachment effort in the House by voting to table it.

articles.title: Top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries 'a hard yes' on impeaching Pete Hegseth
articles.summary: But the Pentagon said the defence secretary would not be deterred by "phony investigations".
articles.body:
The frontrunner to lead the US House of Representatives after Democrats take control of Congress in January has said he is "a hard yes" for impeaching Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries told ABC's programme This Week that Hegseth had "abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran".

Outgoing Republican congressman Thomas Massie, a foe of President Donald Trump, has said he plans to introduce a resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday.

In a statement to the BBC, the Pentagon said it had followed the law and that Hegseth would not be deterred by "phony investigations".

Congress returns to session this week after the Democrats' midterm elections landslide victory.

Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, including accusing him of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 for America's role in the war with Iran.

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution," Jeffries told ABC on Sunday.

"Pete Hegseth has got to go," he continued.

Jeffries - who is favourite to be the next House Speaker, the most powerful member in the lower chamber of Congress - has vowed that the newly empowered Democrats will serve as a check and balance on the Trump administration.

But he said after the midterms results that House Democrats were not currently focused on impeaching President Trump, who was impeached twice during his first term.

Last week, Hegseth released a nearly six-minute video urging Congress to approve the Pentagon's latest military budget request, before the Republican-controlled legislature's final days come to an end.

In the clip, he addressed talks of Massie's impeachment effort, referring to the threat as "sham articles".

"You see, their policies don't work. So, their obsession with political theatre disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents," Hegseth said.

"It's all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn't work against President Trump and it won't work with me."

With more races still to be called, Democrats have a 254-seat majority in the House, well beyond the 218 threshold needed to pass articles of impeachment.

But they will fall well short of the two-thirds Senate majority required to remove an official from office.

articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) on Sunday slammed Trump administration adviser Stephen Miller, who was recently promoted to White House chief of staff, calling him the “most broken man.”

In an interview on ABC News’s “This Week,” the outlet’s Jonathan Karl asked El-Sayed about “what message” Miller’s new role “sends to the country and to your ability to get something done with this White House.”

El-Sayed said that President Trump has expressed wanting to be conciliatory and working with Democrats to deliver on affordability.

“And then he decides to hire the most broken man to continue to run the most dysfunctional White House that we’ve seen, I don’t know what Stephen Miller has actually contributed to our culture, our society in any real way, except for to make us more angry, to stoke the worst kind of fear and vitriol, to weaponize [Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)] in our streets, to take American lives,” he added.

On Friday, Trump announced that chief of staff Susie Wiles was leaving the White House and Miller, a longtime adviser to the president, would take her place.

Miller’s promotion followed Republicans experiencing widespread defeat in the recent midterms, with the House and Senate going to Democrats.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

The Hill has reached out to the White House for comment.

articles.title: After GOP's brutal midterms, ‘Chuck Norris of Florida politics’ tells party to 'get up and fight'
articles.summary: Republican Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by Ron DeSantis, says the GOP must rise like warriors.
articles.body: When an insurgent's bullet shattered his arm in combat, Republican Florida Lt. Gov. Jay Collins did not wait around for an evacuation team; the Green Beret performed emergency surgery on himself to save the limb. After the midterms that Gov. Ron DeSantis called a "near extinction-level" event for Republicans, Collins sees a national GOP lying bloodied on the field. He advises his battered and beaten party to show the same refusal to die, and get up like a warrior. "Where we go from here is up to us as a Republican Party," Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by DeSantis, told Fox News Digital in an interview just days after the midterm "bloodbath." "This can be a definitive death blow if we allow it to be, but I believe in what we stand for." he continued. "I believe in our Constitution. I believe in our founding fathers' vision. I believe that God blessed this nation. I think we have to knuckle down, learn, apply this, and we have come out with a relentless dedication and fury to focus on what matters: To lead our state, to lead our country, and be what we need to be for the American people. That is what we should choose to do." "Hard times happen. Warriors, leaders get up and fight. That's what we have to do now." DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED The metaphor is not subtle. It is a road map, set forth by DeSantis' two four-year terms – the last year of which was supplemented by Collins as his No. 2. HUGH HEWITT: THE GOP IS WOUNDED, NOT DEAD — BUT RECOVERY HAS TO START NOW Collins said his home state's recent history of going from a purple state to a GOP stronghold is an example the rest of the country can follow. "Florida's been the road map," he said. "I think we've been what I call the conservative proving grounds. I think that it's time for many here in Florida to use our voice and to be out there and help our party get back on their feet. Be resilient. Yeah, man, you got popped. You got hurt. Get back up, dust it off, and let's go lead. Let's learn." While congressional Republicans scramble to assign blame for a devastating cycle of national losses – including the loss of Texas to Democrats – Florida has positioned itself as the country’s preeminent conservative fortress, now the largest red state on the 2028 map. "Losing sucks, winning is awesome: Let's get back to more winning," he said. "We've just got to figure out how we're going to do that, and that's achievable. I think Florida is a blueprint. I think we have a responsibility to lead." DAVID MARCUS: HOW ASHLEY MOODY SURVIVED THE BLUE TSUNAMI AND EMERGED AS A GOP STAR Under DeSantis, Florida shed its long-held "purple" swing-state identity to become the nation's largest, most disciplined red bastion. Collins looked back on how he pulled in the no party affiliated voters (NPAs), the valued middle that can flip races and states, in his state Senate race before being tapped to serve under DeSantis. "Republicans showed up, but the NPAs showed up and they overwhelmingly did not align with Republicans," Collins said, admitting that even Florida's heavy Republican registered voter edge led to slim margins in the tough midterm environment. "What does that tell us? Well, the biggest gap we had was that we didn't spend enough time communicating to our NPAs." Collins pointed back to how he won a Tampa race in a district "that is not a conservative juggernaut in terms of Florida," running against the Tampa mayor's mother-in-law. "This was my very first race," he recalled. "We didn't talk to a single Republican out there. We only knocked NPA's and light D's, and we won by 10. What does that tell you? In a community like Tampa, I didn't hide from my views. I told people I'm conservative, I'm a Republican." JASON CHAFFETZ: FIVE TIMELESS POLITICAL LESSONS THAT GOT LOST IN 2026 "What I realized is if you're honest with people, you agree on more than you don't, but you have got to be willing to step in there and have that conversation," he said. "And we did that over and over and again. And we built a base of people who trust us, because I don't play games." "As a party, we need to go back to being the party that welcomes folks in – a little bit more of a big tent – but we have to stand on our conservative values," he added. Collins is termed out of office along with DeSantis in January, but he will evaluate his future in the state or the national party apparatus. For now, he is committing to nothing and merely saying, "Stay tuned." TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING Regardless of candidate or party, Collins goes back to his military background and having risked his life and literally sacrificed limb for unity. "I wore a flag on my shoulder every single day that I served in uniform," he said. "I wore the flag on my suit, really every single day that I was out there, serving in our state or serving our nation in any way that I could. We're the American people; we are blessed." Once the party picks its 2028 candidate, Republicans need to be all-in against the opposition, Collins said. "We have to row the boat," he said. "Sept. 11 was a big day in our life. Sept. 12 was incredible because we saw the power and the might of what America can be. When we rowed the boat, our enemy was fearful. They were on their heels because they saw an absolute juggernaut standing righteously to defend our people and our way of life. What our enemy fears, what other nations fear is Americans coming together." TRUMP-BACKED BYRON DONALDS TO MAKE HISTORY AS FLORIDA’S FIRST BLACK GOVERNOR "We have to come together and realize that our nation is blessed," he continued. "It will fall if we don't come together. But it won't happen if we don't start uniting and remind ourselves that this is America, we're allies, internal in our country, and we're going to make sure that it's the greatest country moving forward. America's worth fighting for." "We need to focus on getting through this, the aftermath of this cycle, wrap it up, transition, and make sure that we understand exactly what happened," he concluded. "You know, when we started the war on terror, and I was a young soldier, we spent two years trying to fight the last war. It wasn't very great, to be honest with you. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Let's not fight the last war. Let's understand the operational environment. Let's under our gaps. Our weaknesses and how we can clearly address those. And then we're going to have to move with a righteous fury."

After the midterms that Gov. Ron DeSantis called a "near extinction-level" event for Republicans, Collins sees a national GOP lying bloodied on the field. He advises his battered and beaten party to show the same refusal to die, and get up like a warrior.

"Where we go from here is up to us as a Republican Party," Collins, dubbed the "Chuck Norris of Florida politics" by DeSantis, told Fox News Digital in an interview just days after the midterm "bloodbath."

"This can be a definitive death blow if we allow it to be, but I believe in what we stand for." he continued. "I believe in our Constitution. I believe in our founding fathers' vision. I believe that God blessed this nation. I think we have to knuckle down, learn, apply this, and we have come out with a relentless dedication and fury to focus on what matters: To lead our state, to lead our country, and be what we need to be for the American people. That is what we should choose to do."

"Hard times happen. Warriors, leaders get up and fight. That's what we have to do now."

The metaphor is not subtle. It is a road map, set forth by DeSantis' two four-year terms – the last year of which was supplemented by Collins as his No. 2.

Collins said his home state's recent history of going from a purple state to a GOP stronghold is an example the rest of the country can follow.

"Florida's been the road map," he said. "I think we've been what I call the conservative proving grounds. I think that it's time for many here in Florida to use our voice and to be out there and help our party get back on their feet. Be resilient. Yeah, man, you got popped. You got hurt. Get back up, dust it off, and let's go lead. Let's learn."

While congressional Republicans scramble to assign blame for a devastating cycle of national losses – including the loss of Texas to Democrats – Florida has positioned itself as the country's preeminent conservative fortress, now the largest red state on the 2028 map.

"Losing sucks, winning is awesome: Let's get back to more winning," he said. "We've just got to figure out how we're going to do that, and that's achievable. I think Florida is a blueprint. I think we have a responsibility to lead."

Under DeSantis, Florida shed its long-held "purple" swing-state identity to become the nation's largest, most disciplined red bastion. Collins looked back on how he pulled in the no party affiliated voters (NPAs), the valued middle that can flip races and states, in his state Senate race before being tapped to serve under DeSantis.

"Republicans showed up, but the NPAs showed up and they overwhelmingly did not align with Republicans," Collins said, admitting that even Florida's heavy Republican registered voter edge led to slim margins in the tough midterm environment. "What does that tell us? Well, the biggest gap we had was that we didn't spend enough time communicating to our NPAs."

Collins pointed back to how he won a Tampa race in a district "that is not a conservative juggernaut in terms of Florida," running against the Tampa mayor's mother-in-law.

"This was my very first race," he recalled. "We didn't talk to a single Republican out there. We only knocked NPA's and light D's, and we won by 10. What does that tell you? In a community like Tampa, I didn't hide from my views. I told people I'm conservative, I'm a Republican."

"What I realized is if you're honest with people, you agree on more than you don't, but you have got to be willing to step in there and have that conversation," he said. "And we did that over and over and again. And we built a base of people who trust us, because I don't play games."

"As a party, we need to go back to being the party that welcomes folks in – a little bit more of a big tent – but we have to stand on our conservative values," he added.

Collins is termed out of office along with DeSantis in January, but he will evaluate his future in the state or the national party apparatus. For now, he is committing to nothing and merely saying, "Stay tuned."

Regardless of candidate or party, Collins goes back to his military background and having risked his life and literally sacrificed limb for unity.

"I wore a flag on my shoulder every single day that I served in uniform," he said. "I wore the flag on my suit, really every single day that I was out there, serving in our state or serving our nation in any way that I could. We're the American people; we are blessed."

Once the party picks its 2028 candidate , Republicans need to be all-in against the opposition, Collins said.

"We have to row the boat," he said. "Sept. 11 was a big day in our life. Sept. 12 was incredible because we saw the power and the might of what America can be. When we rowed the boat, our enemy was fearful. They were on their heels because they saw an absolute juggernaut standing righteously to defend our people and our way of life. What our enemy fears, what other nations fear is Americans coming together."

"We have to come together and realize that our nation is blessed," he continued. "It will fall if we don't come together. But it won't happen if we don't start uniting and remind ourselves that this is America, we're allies, internal in our country, and we're going to make sure that it's the greatest country moving forward. America's worth fighting for."

"We need to focus on getting through this, the aftermath of this cycle, wrap it up, transition, and make sure that we understand exactly what happened," he concluded. "You know, when we started the war on terror, and I was a young soldier, we spent two years trying to fight the last war. It wasn't very great, to be honest with you.

"Let's not fight the last war. Let's understand the operational environment. Let's under our gaps. Our weaknesses and how we can clearly address those. And then we're going to have to move with a righteous fury."

articles.title: 'I'm a hard yes': Hakeem Jeffries announces support for Hegseth impeachment
articles.summary: Jeffries predicted "incredibly strong support" among Democrats for it.
articles.body:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) came out in support of impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth on Sunday, telling ABC News he's a "hard yes."

"I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution. The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe," Jeffries said on ABC's "This Week." "Pete Hegseth has got to go."

Asked by "This Week" co-anchor Jonathan Karl if he's confident all House Democrats will join him in supporting the potential resolution, Jeffries said his conference will "have that conversation" on Tuesday morning, when members convene in Washington for the first time since the midterm election.

"But I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution," Jeffries said.

Kentucky Rep. Thomas Massie, the outgoing Republican lawmaker who has often clashed with President Donald Trump, told ABC News he intends to reintroduce a privileged resolution to impeach Hegseth as early as Monday. By raising a question of privilege on the floor, leaders are required to schedule a vote on it within two legislative days.

Massie's resolution contains eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, accusing the defense secretary of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, in addition to other alleged offenses.

Thus far, Trump has defended Hegseth, telling reporters Thursday that he has "done a fantastic job." The president also told Karl the same day, "I have every intention to keep him."

Hegseth also defended himself Thursday in a video posted on social media.

"A disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice," Hegseth said. "It's all about the politics of personal destruction — didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me."

'Irresponsible' decision to make Stephen Miller chief of staff

Jeffries, who is likely to become the next speaker of the House in January, said Sunday that he has still not spoken to Trump since the midterm elections, which he described as a "tremendous repudiation of MAGA extremism."

"The country clearly has had enough. And we got to fight for an affordable America," Jeffries said. "People are drowning in this failed Republican economy. And enough is enough in that regard. That's why we're going to fight to lower the high cost of living on all the things. And we have to."

While Trump told ABC News in a phone interview after the election that he thinks he can work with Democrats, Jeffries questioned the president's intentions, given his decision announced Friday to elevate White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump loyalist, to the position of White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

"It's an awful choice. Stephen Miller is the architect of Donald Trump's violent mass deportation machine and has unleashed billions of taxpayer dollars to brutalize and kill American citizens, like Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good , and at the same period of time to violently target law-abiding, immigrant families and communities all across the country. So, you know, it was an irresponsible decision in my view," Jeffries said.

"There's not going to be an opportunity, certainly, to work with Stephen Miller and what he represents. And we're committed to forcefully pushing back against the extremism that they may try to continue to unleash on the American people," he added.

Karl pressed Jeffries to clarify if he means that he won't be able to communicate with Miller in the way he sometimes communicated with outgoing chief of staff Wiles.

"It's not going to happen with the new chief of staff to the extent that he lacks -- because he clearly represents, along with Pete Hegseth and a few others, a really toxic brand of political engagement, of politics and of governance. And the American people just voted for that kind of MAGA extremism to be eradicated," Jeffries said.

Democratic priorities for legislation and investigations

Bringing down costs for housing, groceries, gas and healthcare will be top priorities for his party in the new Congress, Jeffries said, as well as ending the war with Iran, stopping "the Trump tariffs," and "[reversing] the Medicaid cuts that put the health insurance of millions of Americans at risk and threatens to close hospitals all over the place."

"The American people clearly want change that's bold, change that's transformational, and change that is dramatic," Jeffries, said, adding "we certainly need to reverse the SNAP cuts, and we need to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits. And hopefully we'll see some courage by a few of our colleagues on the other side of the aisle to work on these issues to get things done."

The Democratic Party is "committed to moving aggressively during the first 100 days of the new Congress and beyond to keep our word," said Jeffries.

According to ABC News national voter polls, 55% of voters who voted for U.S. House races said that government corruption was "crucial" to their vote; another 36% said it was a "major factor."

In a two-word statement released late Tuesday after Democrats were projected to take control of the House, Rep. Robert Garcia, the presumptive chairman of the House Oversight Committee, stated: "Lawyer up."

"Well, there's a cost to corruption. And throughout this campaign we've promised that we would focus certainly on affordability and driving down the high cost of living, and on accountability in the face of the unprecedented corruption that we've seen unleashed on the American people by the Trump cartel," Jeffries said. "We're committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it's found. That's in Congress, in the Supreme Court and with respect to this administration."

For its part, the administration is saying it will investigate Democrats. Trump said Saturday that he ordered the Department of Justice to examine what he deemed "criminal" acts by Democrats, though he did not provide examples to support his allegations. Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday echoed the president's statement.

"What we've seen over the past several days and even over the past several weeks are outright threats, many, many by elected members of Congress and some senators against anybody that's conservative and anybody that that happens to be a Republican," Blanche told CNN. "Over the last several days, we've seen it, that rhetoric even rise up to the point where they're already -- before they're even in power, they're already talking about investigations and impeachments with no basis, no facts, just out there running around -- that that should be something that that President Trump is very concerned about. And certainly I am as well."

articles.title: El-Sayed open to working with Trump on affordable healthcare
articles.summary: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) stated he was open to working with President Trump on affordable healthcare despite the pair trading jabs while the incoming senator was on the campaign trail. “Look, I’ve never met the man. He is the president of the United States. I am the U.S. senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I…
articles.body:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) stated he was open to working with President Trump on affordable healthcare despite the pair trading jabs while the incoming senator was on the campaign trail.

“Look, I’ve never met the man. He is the president of the United States. I am the U.S. senator-elect from the state of Michigan. I am happy to meet with him,” El-Sayed told ABC’s Jonathan Karl on “ This Week .”

“I’ll meet with anyone who can advance the goals I ran on to get money out of politics, put money in pockets, pass Medicare for all,” he continued. “I’ve said this: if he wants to pass Trump Care for All, which will guarantee health care to everyone, and put his name on it, like he’s putting his name on everything, I’m game.”

“Let’s see if he wants to do that. So I haven’t had any outreach. I’m happy to sit down with him, talk about how we can serve the Michiganders who just elected me,” he concluded.

Trump has attacked El-Sayed multiple times about his family background and faith. At a campaign rally, the president told supporters that El-Sayed would be “the only senator that will have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.”

In a Truth Social post before the rally, Trump called El-Sayed “a Jihadist Member of the Muslim Brotherhood,” adding that he believed the incoming Senator wanted “our Country to go to Sharia Law.”

El-Sayed hit back days before Election Day , saying, “I’ll go through a metal detector every day. You sit through a lie detector one time…That’s the deal.”

The Michigan senator’s willingness to work with the president comes after Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas) expressed a similar desire to collaborate with Trump and the MAGA movement on affordable healthcare.

“If the president wants to work with me or with any Democrat to expand healthcare access, I’m there,” Talarico said, adding that he would similarly help to “build millions of new homes” and “slash the red tape.”

Talarico stated that he hoped the midterm election would be a “wake-up call” for Trump and his administration to “reverse course.”

articles.title: White House vows to keep up immigration crackdown after midterms defeat
articles.summary: The Department of Homeland Security also insists it is not backing away on the round-up.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump's administration has vowed not to change course on its mass deportation plans after last week's midterm elections defeat.

"This administration will not slow down its efforts to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens who terrorise our communities," the White House said in a statement to the BBC.

Trump's promotion on Friday of immigration hawk Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff had signalled no climbdown from the administration on border security.

Exit polls indicate immigration was the third most important issue for midterm voters, after the economy and the state of democracy.

In historically conservative states like Texas, a swing of Latino voters towards Democrats helped seal the party's landslide congressional majorities.

But multiple US officials sources told the BBC's US partner CBS that the administration had put the midterm losses down to concerns about the economy, affordability and the war with Iran, rather than its immigration crackdown.

The White House maintained on Sunday there would be no change of direction.

"There has never been a President stronger on immigration enforcement than President Trump," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also said it would forge ahead.

"ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down," a DHS spokesperson told CBS.

"Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation's laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets."

Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US

Following Tuesday's results, Vice-President JD Vance had appeared receptive to adjusting their immigration strategy.

"I'm open to the idea that we should change enforcement - by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labour, for instance," Vance wrote in a lengthy online post reflecting on the results.

But the White House's posture appears to have hardened after Trump promoted Stephen Miller on Friday to become his new chief of staff.

Miller is widely seen as the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policy during the first and second Trump presidencies.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) sources told CBS that in recent weeks officials have been instructed to aim for about 2,700 arrests of illegal immigrants per day, an increase from an earlier 2,000 daily arrest target.

Enforcement sweeps this year spurred anti-ICE demonstrations in cities including Chicago, Minneapolis and Los Angeles.

In Minneapolis, two US protesters, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were fatally shot by immigration agents.

articles.title: Donalds says GOP must campaign on new healthcare policy in 2028
articles.summary: Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds (R) on Sunday said the Republican Party will have to campaign with its own crafted healthcare policy items going into the 2028 election. Donalds told Fox News’s interim host of “Sunday Morning Futures” Larry Kudlow that Republican lawmakers on Capitol Hill are having “many debates” about taking on healthcare, adding that…
articles.body:
Florida Gov.-elect Byron Donalds (R) on Sunday said the Republican Party will have to campaign with its own crafted healthcare policy items going into the 2028 election.

Donalds told Fox News’s interim host of “Sunday Morning Futures” Larry Kudlow that Republican lawmakers on Capitol Hill are having “many debates” about taking on healthcare, adding that Republican leaders “did not want to take healthcare on.”

“We need market-centered healthcare policy that will stabilize prices in healthcare and drive down costs in healthcare,” he said. “And Republicans, I think, for ’28 and beyond, we need to step into that breach and say, ‘Here’s how you actually get it done on healthcare.’ Because if we continue under Democrat policy, it’s going to continue to price out hardworking families all across America.”

He noted reporting from the New York Times about ObamaCare premiums increasing by an average of 13 percent in 2027, adding that the U.S. has been “under Democrat policy and healthcare” for the past 15 years.

“The premiums are out of control, the deductibles are out of control, the costs are out of control. And now you have Bernie Sanders and the left –– they’re talking about Medicare for All,” Donalds said, referring to the independent Vermont senator and his core policy issue of single-payer healthcare.

Voters offered a strong rebuke of the GOP health agenda after Democrats made healthcare affordability a major issue on the campaign trail. They campaigned on restoring the enhanced Affordable Care Act subsidies and on delaying or rolling back the Medicaid cuts passed under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

The sweeping wins were also a rebuke of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda, touted by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the Trump administration’s health policies.

Tuesday’s victories also pushed forward more talk about a future where “Medicare for All” can be discussed, with victories of candidates like Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) and other progressives in the House and Senate who are expected to make a significant push for single-payer healthcare.

As many adults and families struggle to afford health costs, the popularity of Medicare for All is growing. A KFF poll in September showed two-thirds of Americans favored a “single government plan.”

President Trump entered office having told voters that he had the “framework of a plan” for healthcare, after his previous healthcare plan was defeated during his first term.

With the president’s last two years of his second term in focus, El-Sayed told ABC’s Jonathan Karl on “ This Week ” that he would work with him on affordable healthcare despite the two taking sharp jabs at each other during this past election cycle.

“I’ve said this: if he wants to pass Trump Care for All, which will guarantee health care to everyone, and put his name on it, like he’s putting his name on everything, I’m game,” El-Sayed said.

articles.title: Deputy White House Chief of Staff Richard Walters exits job ahead of Stephen Miller takeover
articles.summary: Stephen Miller praised Richard Walters as an “invaluable member" who will continue helping the administration from outside the White House.
articles.body: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Richard Walters, a longtime ally of outgoing White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, is leaving the Trump administration following President Donald Trump's decision to replace Wiles with Stephen Miller. Miller confirmed Walters' departure in a statement to Fox News, describing him as an "invaluable member" of the White House who will continue to assist the administration from the outside. TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES "Richard has been an invaluable member of the White House and has helped deliver some of the Administration’s biggest victories. While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to Save America," Miller said. The departure marks another major staffing shakeup as Trump moves to reshape his team following the midterm election results. Miller is expected to install his own leadership team when he takes over Monday. Miller's wife, Katie, on Sunday also announced that she would stop recording new episodes of her show, The Katie Miller Podcast, where she interviews political figures, athletes and other public personalities. She said the decision was based on what was best for her children and family as her husband's new role brings a shift in priorities. "With @StephenM taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop recording new podcast episodes," Katie said in a post on X. "Nothing is more important than raising our four kids. While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away. I’ll be cheering President Trump and his team on from outside the administration," she added. articles.title: Nvidia launches investigation into CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
articles.summary: Jensen Huang also admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and says he will cooperate with a security investigation.
articles.body:
US tech giant Nvidia has opened an independent investigation following reports its CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company, one of the most valuable in the world, said its board had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, adding that the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company.

Separately, Jensen Huang admitted to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Huang, was a spy for China's Ministry of State Security, according to a New York Times report.

Jensen Huang said he took "full responsibility" for what he did, and said he had fallen short of his responsibilities to Nvidia's employees, board and shareholders.

Nvidia is one of the world's largest companies and seen as central to making the hardware for emerging AI technologies.

Its CEO said: "I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry."

His statement continued: "Regarding the national security concerns raised in news reports, Nvidia's Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully.

"I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American."

A separate statement issued by Nvidia's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

It continued: "The Board prioritises US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders.

"While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the Board's inquiry will examine all available information."

Alice Huang is linked to Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, providing chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

The microchip manufacturer is worth some $4.5 trillion, making it one of the most valuable companies ever.

China has previously rejected allegations of an espionage operation targeting Nvidia's chief, describing the claims as "groundless speculation" .

US intelligence agencies had been monitoring Alice Huang and concluded that she was acting on behalf of the Chinese government, according to unnamed sources cited by The New York Times.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what information Alice Huang - who is also known as Huang Le - allegedly passed to Beijing, how valuable it was, or when she is believed to have begun gathering intelligence.

Alice Huang did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

Last week, members of Congress wrote to Jensen Huang, asking him to appear before them in the light of the reported relationship.

Three House Republican committee leaders asked the CEO to appear later in the month, to talk about Nvidia's "security protocols against foreign adversary espionage" given his reported relation Alice Huang.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information.

"The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge US technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress," the letter said.

Nvidia's AI chips have been a major focus of the rivalry between the US and China, and Washington has previously imposed controls on where its advanced products can be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted by Washington over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

articles.title: Mamdani: Abolishing ICE is the most ‘acceptable’ part of DSA platform to ‘mainstream America’
articles.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said that of all the platform items belonging to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), of which he is a member, the most “acceptable part” for “mainstream America” is abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Mamdani appeared on “Fox News Sunday” for an interview recorded Wednesday night with…
articles.body:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) said that of all the platform items belonging to the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), of which he is a member, the most “acceptable part” for “mainstream America” is abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

Mamdani appeared on “Fox News Sunday” for an interview recorded Wednesday night with Shannon Bream, who pointed to various DSA policy items that Americans may not favor. She asked what part of the platform the mayor thinks is acceptable to mainstream Americans.

“Look, I think the thing that is most acceptable to mainstream America is abolishing ICE and making sure we have humanity back in our immigration enforcement,” Mamdani said. “And the thing that has been offered as a part of a litany of policy platforms that I would reject is after last night, why would we abolish the Senate?”

Mamdani referred to several candidates who he said that “no matter how they describe themselves,” they ran “on policies that would transform working people’s lives.” He referred to Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-S.C.) and Georgia Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms (D) as examples.

Bream ran through other DSA policy proposals with the mayor, including the abolition of the Supreme Court, prisons and borders, all of which Mamdani said “no” to.

“So, do you think DSA’s going to kick you out?” she asked the mayor as he smiled back. “It sounds like you’re not aligned with some of the core things they really want to get done.”

“No. You know, when you go into a room and there are more than one socialist in the room, you will often find disagreement in that room,” he replied. “And what unites members of the Democratic Socialists of America is, in many ways, what has brought people into politics over the years –– a belief in the dignity of working class people and the dignity that has to be a characteristic of their lives.”

He said that the work that goes into democracy must be “meaningful” and does not end at the ballot box but for “the rest of our lives, from the workplace to every other aspect of it.”

Democratic socialist candidates made major victories across the country, including with two more mayoral victories like Mamdani’s. Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George (D) will become Washington, D.C.’s next mayor , and DSA member and Los Angeles City Council member Nithya Raman (D) will become the City of Angels’s next mayor, defeating incumbent Mayor Karen Bass (D).

Democratic candidates have also targeted ICE as they campaigned this past year, overwhelmingly criticizing President Trump’s immigration crackdown and his deportation agenda. They have vowed to use their power in Congress to restrain ICE, potentially withholding future funding and becoming an authority to conduct oversight on the agency.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, however, vowed last Wednesday to continue deporting those detained by ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officers.

articles.title: Trump says he’s ‘unlikely’ to renew attacks on Iran if talks show progress
articles.summary: President Trump said he was “highly unlikely” to renew attacks against Iran if upcoming peace talks show progress regarding Tehran’s nuclear program and opening the Strait of Hormuz, according to a new CNN report. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said during an interview with CNN’s Jim Sciutto.…
articles.body:
President Trump said he was “highly unlikely” to renew attacks against Iran if upcoming peace talks show progress regarding Tehran’s nuclear program and opening the Strait of Hormuz, according to a new CNN report .

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump said during an interview with CNN’s Jim Sciutto. “The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”

“So it’s highly unlikely I’ll have to,” he continued while on the phone with Sciutto. “They’re withering away financially. We’ve hit them militarily. We could finish them off.”

Trump added that “most likely it will not be necessary” to renew military action because “they want to make a deal so badly.”

The U.S. reportedly launched new defensive strikes against Iran over the weekend that targeted the country’s air defense systems. The president described the attack as “minor” on Friday.

They followed up on alleged attacks from Nov. 2 that struck Iran’s Qeshm Island, home to an Iranian naval base and located in the critical Strait of Hormuz. The strikes ahead of the midterms were not publicly acknowledged by the Pentagon, which had not disclosed any attacks on Iranian targets since early September.

Trump had previously said he would not strike Iran until after the midterms.

During the interview, Trump confirmed that the U.S. had identified “38 bridges” and other infrastructure projects to target if Iran decided to relaunch attacks, but he reiterated he doesn’t “want to do that because essentially, it’ll take 10 years to rebuild them.”

“I don’t like ripping down bridges. And the hardest thing to build is a bridge. It takes years, and I’m a good builder,” he continued.

The Iran war is wildly unpopular among the American public, as an October Reuters/Ipsos survey reported that just 33 percent of Americans approved of the Iran war, while 62 percent disapproved.

articles.title: White House deputy chief of staff departs under Miller shakeup
articles.summary: White House deputy chief of staff Richard Walters is departing from his role in the wake of longtime Trump adviser Stephen Miller being announced as the new chief of staff. “Richard has been an invaluable member of the White House and has helped deliver some of the Administration’s biggest victories,” Miller said in a statement…
articles.body:
White House deputy chief of staff Richard Walters is departing from his role in the wake of longtime Trump adviser Stephen Miller being announced as the new chief of staff.

“Richard has been an invaluable member of the White House and has helped deliver some of the Administration’s biggest victories,” Miller said in a statement obtained by The Hill’s sister network NewsNation.

“While he will be leaving us, Richard will continue to help from the outside as we continue to work with all of our strength to deliver for President Trump and his courageous fight to Save America,” he added.

Last week , Trump announced that chief of staff Susie Wiles was leaving the White House and Miller would take her place.

Miller’s promotion came after a rough Election Day for Republicans, with Democrats taking the House and Senate and winning in regions where they have historically struggled.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

articles.title: Democrats see new path to expand Senate majority in 2028
articles.summary: Democrats’ sweeping victory Tuesday has scrambled conventional wisdom around the 2028 Senate map. Emboldened party leaders see the world as their oyster and are looking ahead to expanding their majority with a map where suddenly anything seems possible. “Some of the very same states where we won this election will offer new opportunities to…
articles.body:
Democrats’ sweeping victory Tuesday has scrambled conventional wisdom around the 2028 Senate map.

Emboldened party leaders see the world as their oyster and are looking ahead to expanding their majority with a map where suddenly anything seems possible.

“Some of the very same states where we won this election will offer new opportunities to expand our majority in 2028 — Iowa, Kansas, the Carolinas and more,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) said during an event Thursday.

“We need to start identifying now in 2027, to solidify our position in the states we won and build our party infrastructure in those areas and continue to expand the map into new states,” Schumer added.

There are only three Democratic senators up for reelection in 2028 that are from battleground states: Georgia, Ohio and Pennsylvania.

Democrats won big in all three of them Tuesday.

The party is also strongly positioned in blue or purple states where an incumbent is up for reelection: California, Oregon, Washington, Colorado, Nevada, Illinois, Hawaii, New York and several New England states.

Meanwhile, Republicans have a steeper battle, and seats once thought as safely red may not be anymore.

They’re defending singular Senate seats in both Carolinas, Iowa and Kansas after Democratic flips. Similarly, they will have to defend seats in Wisconsin and Indiana after Democrats won statewide.

Democrats remain within striking distance in Alaska of unseating Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) as the vote tabulating process continues. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R) is up for reelection there in two years.

While Republicans held serve in Florida , Democrats made significant inroads in the Sunshine State, and it could be competitive in 2028.

Tommy Garcia, a spokesperson for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, was less bullish but said in a statement that Democrats had transformed “a difficult map.”

“We had incredible candidates who ran strong campaigns laser-focused on the issues that matter most to voters, and now they will use their majority in the Senate to fight for lower costs and to root out corruption,” Garcia said.

To succeed over the next two years and avoid pitfalls, operatives say national Democratic organizations need to spend like no state is off limits, especially in the South.

Both Carolinas, Florida, Georgia, Texas and Mississippi were extremely competitive this cycle. Democrats won Senate seats in each of them except Florida, while Mississippi’s race was too close to call by press time.

Christale Spain, South Carolina Democratic Party chair, said a Democrat winning the state for the first time in nearly 20 years will make it easier to recruit candidates to challenge Sen. Tim Scott (R) next cycle.

But she said the national party will need to devote resources to maintain its newfound success.

“I think that in order for us to duplicate or even do even better than we did Tuesday night was that we’re going to have to have a lot of national investment,” Spain said.

“We’ve learned as a state party to do more with less, but in order to continue this momentum, we’ve got to have investment from other national organizations other than just the DNC [Democratic National Committee],” Spain said. “They’ve been a great partner, but we’re going to have to see just more substantial, sustained national investment.”

Democrats in Florida are also making the case that national investment would have helped them get even further: They broke the GOP’s statewide supermajority while still falling short of winning the gubernatorial race or the Senate race.

Incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody (Fla.), who defeated Angie Nixon on Tuesday in a special election to finish the remainder of Marco Rubio’s term, will have to be elected again in 2028 to serve a full term.

Nixon said she is keeping the door open to challenging Moody again in two years.

Florida Democratic Party Chair Nikki Fried said she’s been spreading the word that Florida needs more national money and attention for Democrats to have a shot at 2028.

“I think the biggest takeaway from looking at the rest of the map is that all the states that flipped had national presence, national resources, and people just abandoned us, and so we had to fight to get out of this mess by ourselves,” Fried said.

That kind of investment is part of how Democrats succeeded in races in North Carolina and Georgia, once thought to be among the toughest for Democrats.

A year ago, most election experts thought North Carolina’s Senate race would be one of the most competitive in the cycle.

But in the final months, it became clear that Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper was likely to win, and national groups began shifting money elsewhere.

Cooper is well known in the state and has never lost an election. His campaign focused heavily on its “Make Stuff Cost Less” slogan and kept Cooper out of the headlines.

“No matter what shiny objects were floating around in the national media, this was always about making this a North Carolina-centric campaign,” said Jeff Allen, Cooper’s campaign manager. “And so, to me, that’s one of the takeaways because it also made sure that we never forgot that North Carolina, at its core, is a 50-50 state.”

Allen said there’s plenty of room to run a similar play to unseat Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) in two years. He cited an AARP poll from September that showed Budd’s approval rating at 28 percent.

“Ted Budd is not well liked in this state, and North Carolina Republicans, I think, know that,” Allen said. “I think there is a real opportunity to flip this seat, and we’ve obviously got to continue figuring out what the best path is for ‘28 and down the line, but I think that we have a lot that we can learn from this cycle.”

Georgia was another state that turned out less competitive this year than expected.

Incumbent Sen. Jon Ossoff (D) was considered to be the most vulnerable senator in the chamber at the outset of the campaign, when the 2024 “red wave” still loomed large. But Ossoff won by nearly 20 points .

Yet for all the Democratic hopes, there are Republican targets up for reelection, too.

In Ohio, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is about to retake a Senate seat, but only for two years. Republicans successfully ousted him in 2024, and the right candidate could do so again.

Georgia’s other Senate seat, held by Sen. Raphael Warnock (D), could be one of the GOP’s better hopes for a pickup in 2028. But it won’t be easy.

Warnock could be tough to beat, said Ryan Mahoney, a Republican strategist in Georgia, since he’s a disciplined campaigner with strong constituent services.

In addition, much of Warnock’s “dirty laundry,” including potentially controversial statements from his sermons as a pastor, came out during his 2020 campaign against Kelly Loeffler.

“All of the things that are going to be said about Warnock have been said before and didn’t work,” said Mahoney, who was Loeffler’s communications director at the time. “So I think for Republicans they do need to hope that he isn’t as precise and strategic and intentional as Ossoff, because he goes into reelection in a really good spot with people not thinking he’s as progressive as he actually is deep down.”

Still, Mahoney said if Democrats take their newfound majority too far at the federal or state levels there will be more opportunities for Republicans.

“Democrats do not have a mandate in Georgia, and if they believe that they do, and if they act like they do, they will lose,” Mahoney said.
