articles.title: This week on the Hill: Congress returns to leadership fights, shutdown deadline after GOP losses
articles.summary: Congress returns to Capitol Hill after an astonishing midterm election that dealt Republicans major losses and left Democrats riding high. Now, Republicans face their next major test: a fight over who will lead the party in the House as it prepares its descent into the minority. House Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections…
articles.body:
Congress returns to Capitol Hill after an astonishing midterm election that dealt Republicans major losses and left Democrats riding high. Now, Republicans face their next major test: a fight over who will lead the party in the House as it prepares its descent into the minority.

House Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections Nov. 10. Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) told lawmakers on a staff call last week that he will not run for minority leader, setting the stage for a potentially bruising contest between House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) and House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio).

Republican Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) are both seeking to retain their leadership positions in the minority. But neither is guaranteed a smooth path, with both facing challengers from within the conference.

Johnson has more than a leadership transition to contend with during the final weeks of the congressional session.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) will reintroduce articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth this week, largely over his handling of the war in Iran. Several Republicans, including Vice President Vance, have pointed to the conflict as a reason for the party’s election losses, though they have stopped short of calling for Hegseth’s ouster.

Congress also faces a looming Dec. 11 government funding deadline. Lawmakers must either pass all 12 annual appropriations bills or pass another stopgap measure to avert a shutdown, adding another major legislative hurdle to an already compressed lame-duck session.

The Senate, meanwhile, is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on advancing a bipartisan permitting reform package that would speed up the build-out of the nation’s infrastructure, especially energy projects.

GOP leadership elections heat up: Jordan and Scalise are vying for minority leader, a position that will play a key role in countering the Democratic agenda next year.

Massie to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth: The Defense Secretary has faced scrutiny from the Kentucky Republican and Democrats over his handling of the Iran war and other ventures.

Lawmakers race to avert shutdown: Republicans and Democrats have only a few weeks to pass a stopgap measure or complete work on all 12 appropriations bills before Dec. 11.

Senate to take up bipartisan permitting reform bill: The legislation, which would make it harder to block energy projects, is expected to advance.

Republicans have been divided over how to move forward as a conference, with some arguing that there needs to be a complete revamp of the leadership team.

“There has to be accountability for results, and you know the team that led us to the disaster probably isn’t the team that should lead us from the disaster,” one GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, told The Hill.

Jordan, co-founder of the far-right House Freedom Caucus, has emerged as a favorite among some House Republicans.

“I think we’re going into a wartime situation where we are going to be the rebel alliance, and we’re going to need someone who knows how to fight, and Jim Jordan knows how to do that,” the lawmaker said.

House Freedom Caucus Chair Andy Harris (R-Md.) also threw his support behind Jordan, arguing on Newsmax Thursday that Jordan “is the type of communicator we need, communicating common-sense Republican conservative principles again, against the backdrop of what is going to be a DSA-dominated Senate and House Democrat majority.”

But other Republicans argue that Scalise is better positioned to take the top spot, given his current leadership role. Scalise initially won the Republican nomination to be Speaker in 2023, beating Jordan in a secret-ballot vote. But he withdrew from the race when it became clear he would not win enough support from his conference to get the votes needed on the House floor.

“Steve is the right guy for the job. Plain and simple. He’s a tried and tested leader, who has the experience to lead House Republicans for the next two years, and the chops to reclaim the majority in 2028,” a second GOP lawmaker, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said.

Republican Study Committee Chair August Pfluger (R-Texas) is challenging Emmer for the minority whip position, while Reps. Greg Steube (R-Fla.) and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) are going head-to-head against McClain for the GOP conference chair role.

Massie to reintroduce articles of impeachment on Hegseth

Massie said on X last week that he plans to reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth unless the defense secretary resigns. Most Democrats are expected to support the measure, but House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) has stopped short of endorsing it.

Massie had previously launched an effort to impeach Hegseth back in September, but House GOP leaders canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early, avoiding a vote on Massie’s resolution. But only temporarily.

The Kentucky Republican argued then that Hegseth violated “his oath to support and defend the Constitution of the United States” and violated “his constitutional duty to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, especially with regard to the commission of war.” He added that Hegseth has “abused the powers of the Department of Defense.”

President Trump told ABC News’s Jonathan Karl last week that he has “every intention” of keeping Hegseth in the Cabinet, following reports that he was weighing whether the Defense chief should stay in the post after the midterm elections.

Hegseth also fired back at Massie last week, saying in a video clip posted to X that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly.”

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction,” Hegseth said. “Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that.”

He’s probably right on that score. Even if the House does impeach Hegseth, the Senate is not likely to remove him from power.

Lawmakers work to avert government shutdown in December

Lawmakers have just two weeks to make progress on government funding before leaving again for Thanksgiving recess — an effort that will be challenged by a crowded legislative agenda that includes the annual National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), a farm bill and other priorities.

The House has passed three of the 12 appropriations bills, while Senate appropriators have remained deadlocked over top-line spending levels. The bills the House has passed so far — funding military construction and the Department of Veterans Affairs, the State Department, and agriculture and rural development — represent some of the lowest-hanging fruit.

Johnson is sure to face much tougher resistance — both from Democrats and within his party — when the topic shifts to funding other agencies, including the departments of Homeland Security, Defense and Health and Human Services.

Democratic lawmakers told The Hill before the midterms that they are keen on getting the rest of the appropriations bills done. But with a short calendar and a contentious subject, the odds are stacked against them. Most observers think a short-term spending patch, known as a continuing resolution, or CR, is the most likely scenario.

House Appropriations Committee ranking member Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.) told The Hill in a statement she doesn’t think anyone wants a shutdown, and one is not likely.

“Both Democrats and Republicans have expressed a desire to finish full-year funding bills before the end of this calendar year, and I am ready to do just that,” DeLauro said. “The American people want us to address the cost of living crisis and rein in this corrupt administration. With Democrats widely expected to be in the majority, we want to hit the ground running in the new year — not be forced to finish the work this Congress failed to complete.”

Rep. Andrew Clyde (R-Ga.), a member of the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement before the midterms that “whether or not there is a government shutdown is entirely up to Senate Democrats, who inflicted the longest government shutdown in U.S. history on the American people last year.”

“My priority remains passing the most conservative and fiscally responsible appropriations bills possible, and I look forward to completing that work when we return to Washington in the coming weeks,” he added.

Senate to hold procedural vote on bipartisan permitting reform bill

The upper chamber is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on a permitting reform bill, dubbed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act.

The legislation would make changes to the nation’s environmental laws that could make it easier to build projects and make it harder to block them, with either lawsuits or other legal mechanisms.

It also has provisions that are expected to make it easier to build and approve power lines, in particular, which is key to getting more power onto the grid. Democrats have pushed for such reforms, saying they believe they will particularly bolster renewable energy.

Trump has gone after renewable energy projects, and the bill contains measures that would protect those that are already approved. This bill could prevent Trump or other Republicans from trying to cancel renewable projects.

The bill is expected to advance, but it could receive some pushback from progressive Senate Democrats who have called for the administration to restore climate funding it terminated for blue states.

“While such action may not fully address the wide range of concerns individual Senators have about various portions of this complex legislation, it would represent an important first step and carry far more weight with us and, more importantly, our constituents whose awards were illegally terminated, than mere informal assurances that the Trump administration will stop interfering with clean energy projects,” the liberal senators wrote in a letter to Democratic and Republican negotiators of the bill.

Rachel Frazin contributed to this report.

articles.title: Popular progressive podcast sees sponsors flee after ‘insensitive’ Charlie Kirk joke
articles.summary: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan, hosts of the ‘I’ve Had It’ podcast, have apologized for laughing at a joke about the slain conservative influencer
articles.body:
A popular progressive podcast has seen its sponsors flee after laughing at a joke about the slain conservative influencer Charlie Kirk , which the hosts later admitted was "insensitive."

Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan read social media posts reacting to Tuesday's midterm election — in which Democrats took control of the House and Senate and won key governors' races — on Thursday's episode of their I've Had It podcast.

They both cracked up to a post that read, "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again."

The clip has since been cut from the episode, and the two apologized for laughing at the joke. But the damage has already been done.

Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk , blasted "leftist podcasters" and others who laugh about political assassination "beyond disgusting" in an X post Sunday.

When an outraged social media user told his followers to boycott Cash App for sponsoring "these rotten women," the peer-to-peer payment platform wrote on X Friday, "We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast."

Pet brand Chewy announced Saturday that it currently has no ties to the podcast.

"We do not sponsor or support the 'I've Had It' podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy's values or what we stand for as a company," Chewy wrote on X.

Eyewear brand Zenni also announced that it "does not condone violence of any type."

"We have canceled advertising on I've Had It and are reviewing our podcast placements against our brand safety standards," Zenni wrote on X.

Organic bedding brand Boll & Branch said it "does not currently advertise with the 'I've Had It' podcast and will not in the future."

Kirk, the founder of the conservative youth organization Turning Point USA, was assassinated at age 31 during an outdoor event on a college campus in Utah in September 2025.

Both Republicans and Democrats condemned the assassination of Kirk, who was seen as a steward of Trump's MAGA movement and even a potential presidential nominee in the future. Some critics made light of or even celebrated Kirk's death, and they were swiftly rebuked.

Amid backlash for their response to a joke about Kirk's assassination, Welch and Sullivan wrote on Instagram, "On Thursday's show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize."

"Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We've long supported common-sense gun safety reform," the hosts said. "To that end, we've made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America. We'll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans."

articles.title: Katie Miller pauses podcast after husband named White House chief of staff
articles.summary: After Stephen Miller was selected as White House chief of staff, his wife, conservative influencer Katie Miller, said she is stepping back from her podcast on Sunday. “I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family. With @StephenM taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop…
articles.body:
After Stephen Miller was selected as White House chief of staff, his wife, conservative influencer Katie Miller, said she is stepping back from her podcast on Sunday.

“I make every decision based on what’s best for my children and our family. With @StephenM taking on this new role for President Trump, I’ve decided to stop recording new podcast episodes,” Miller said in a post to the social platform X .

“Nothing is more important than raising our four kids. While I’ve loved the podcast, the time commitment is too great and now is the time to step away. I’ll be cheering President Trump and his team on from outside the administration,” she continued

Miller added that she “will be airing the two previously taped episodes” of The Katie Miller Podcast.

Miller’s podcast launched in 2025, and guests have included right-leaning figures like Elon Musk and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. The most recent episode of the podcast was released on Oct. 27 .

Trump announced on Friday that chief of staff Susie Wiles was leaving the White House and Stephen Miller, a longtime adviser to the president, would take her place.

Stephen Miller’s promotion followed a shellacking for Republicans on Election Day last week, with Democrats seizing the House and Senate.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

“Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation,” he continued. “I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

articles.title: Jeffries backs Hegseth impeachment as Democrats vow probes of Trump allies
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers are mapping out their post-midterm agenda with pledges to lead committee investigations into Trump.
articles.body:
United States House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has thrown his support behind impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, as the Democratic Party prepares to use its incoming congressional majorities to probe President Donald Trump’s administration.

In a Sunday appearance on the Television show This Week with George Stephanopoulos, Jeffries weighed in on the upcoming impeachment resolution, anticipated for the coming days.

“I’m a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said. “The so-called secretary of defence has abused his power, undermined our national security, and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran.”

The impeachment resolution has been spearheaded by outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a vocal critic of the US-Israel war on Iran .

“Pete Hegseth has got to go,” Jeffries added. “I believe there will be incredibly strong support for that resolution.”

Investigating ‘unprecedented corruption’

Jeffries is poised to become the next speaker in the House of Representatives after Democrats notched a historic victory in the November 3 midterm elections.

Both the House and the Senate flipped into Democratic control, with the left-wing party making some of its biggest gains in the lower chamber in more than half a century.

Democrats are expected to use their new congressional majorities to launch investigations into the Trump administration.

There have also been concerns, voiced by Trump himself, that he and other top officials could face impeachment.

In Sunday’s interview, Jeffries said the Democratic majority would move “aggressively” in its first 100 days in office, both to address affordability and “unprecedented corruption” under Trump.

“We are committed to cleaning up the mess wherever it’s found,” Jeffries said. “That’s in Congress, in the Supreme Court, and with respect to this administration.”

Currently, Republicans hold a government “trifecta”, with control of both chambers of Congress and the presidency. The Supreme Court also boasts a conservative supermajority, shaped by three Trump appointees.

But a new Congress will be sworn in on January 3. In the coming weeks, Democrats will choose their party leaders for both chambers.

Representative Robert Garcia formally announced his bid to lead the House Oversight Committee in a letter to colleagues on Thursday.

The committee is the chamber’s principal investigative panel, with the power to subpoena witnesses and documents.

On Sunday, Garcia told CNN that Stephen Miller ‘s influential role in the Trump administration warranted investigation.

Miller, who was named last week as White House chief of staff, has been closely associated with Trump’s hardline immigration policies since his first term as president.

“What we think is that Stephen Miller is the architect of this horrific, unjust policy happening across the country,” Garcia said, pointing to policies of separating immigrant families and accusations of due process abuses.

“Stephen Miller is at the centre of major policy decisions that are happening in the administration, and it does deserve oversight and investigation.”

Garcia also signalled interest in questioning businessman Elon Musk over his leadership in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a federal initiative that led to widespread federal workforce cuts at the start of Trump’s second term.

DOGE also sought access to sensitive government data, including Americans’ personal information.

“What happened with DOGE, in particular, and the federal employees losing jobs the way they did and people’s data likely being compromised, I think, is very serious,” Garcia said.

Congressional committees have the power to hold hearings, subpoena witnesses, and demand documents, giving lawmakers a constitutional check on the executive branch.

The House can also impeach administration officials if a simple majority votes in favour.

Conviction and removal, however, require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a high bar even with Democrats controlling the chamber.

The White House was quick to draw its own battle lines.

Speaking on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday, Attorney General Todd Blanche said there could be investigations into Democratic lawmakers over their “threatening” rhetoric.

He added he was ready to counter Democratic efforts to probe and impeach Trump officials.

“If that’s what this new incoming leadership wants to do, we are ready,” said Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump. “If you work in this administration, you have a lawyer. It’s me.”

Trump, meanwhile, made similar remarks in a Truth Social post on Saturday.

He called on the Justice Department to investigate Democrats over their plans to haul his allies before congressional committees, branding them as “SLEAZEBAGS” who “should go to jail”.

“The threats being made by the Democrat Party against innocent Republican Donors and Party Members are absolutely unprecedented, and totally illegal,” the president wrote.

articles.title: Rep.-elect says Democratic majority is an ‘opportunity’ for Trump
articles.summary: Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) said Sunday that the Democrats’ upcoming majority in Congress provides a chance for President Trump to work with the party to improve Americans’ lives. “But make no mistake about it, if we don’t get to Washington, D.C., and we don’t start pushing legislation that elevates people’s lives, we’re going to lose…
articles.body:
Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.) said Sunday that the Democrats’ upcoming majority in Congress provides a chance for President Trump to work with the party to improve Americans’ lives.

“But make no mistake about it, if we don’t get to Washington, D.C., and we don’t start pushing legislation that elevates people’s lives, we’re going to lose that in two years,” Ojeda told NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday.” “So, if we want to stay, we got to do the right things for the people.”

“But you can’t do too many things because Donald Trump’s going to veto. If you do those things, he’s going to veto those things,” Stirewalt replied.

“This is an opportunity. This is an opportunity for Donald Trump. And I would say — if I was talking to him, I would say, ‘This is an opportunity for you. Instead of basically going out as a lame duck and doing nothing and making this just absolutely petty, how about support the legislation that elevates people’s lives?” Ojeda said.

Ojeda beat Rep. Richard Hudson (R), the chair of the National Republican Congressional Committee (NRCC), in the race for North Carolina’s 9th Congressional District last week.

In his NRCC role, Hudson had to help protect at-risk House Republicans throughout the U.S. He also had to set aside some resources for his own campaign, per Cook Political Report. However, Ojeda won, and his victory was the first for a Democrat in the district since 1963.

The Congressional map was painted blue in this year’s midterm elections, with Democrats locking down the House and Senate and flipping historically red areas.

On Tuesday, Trump congratulated Democrats for their election wins. In a call with CBS News, the president said that his message was “congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country.”

articles.title: Joe Biden says cancer slowed him down, limiting memoir promotion tour
articles.summary: Former President Joe Biden revealed his prostate cancer battle will limit promotional events for his presidential memoir, "Promise Me, America," out Nov. 17.
articles.body: Former President Joe Biden said on Sunday ahead of the release of his presidential memoir that he would need to limit the promotional events due to his cancer battle slowing him down at times. The memoir, titled "Promise Me, America," is set to be released on Nov. 17. The book reflects on Biden's four years in the White House, covering the COVID-19 pandemic, the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, domestic legislation, global diplomacy and his decision to run for re-election before later stepping aside in 2024. The memoir also details the personal deliberations behind his decision to end his 2024 re-election bid. "My presidential memoir, PROMISE ME, AMERICA, is coming out on November 17th. I hope you'll read it. It covers my years as President. The challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them. It's about who we are as a nation. What we stand for. And America's role in the world. More than anything, it's about my faith in the American people and the great American experiment in self-governance and democracy," Biden said on X. JOE BIDEN'S CANCER HAS SPREAD FURTHER, LEAVING HIM IN 'VERY PAINFUL' CONDITION, HUNTER REVEALS The former president was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones in May 2025, which he said has not stopped him but has sometimes slowed him down. "While writing the book, I was diagnosed with cancer, a disease known all too well to millions of Americans and their families. My doctors continue to be encouraged by how I've responded to treatment. And the prayers and kind words and well wishes from so many of you have meant more to me and Jill and our family than you can ever know," Biden said. "Some days are better than others. articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday said his deportation policies might have been “too tough” and led to the GOP’s historic losses in this year’s elections.

CBS News’s Ross Douthat asked the president on “60 Minutes” if his immigration policy lost his party the midterms.

“I think it both helped and hurt,” Trump responded. “I think I got an A plus for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out, but I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation for breaking of the law, that was what they came into the country illegally.”

“Now, there is a large part of the country that think that they should be put out,” he continued. “And there’s a large part of the country that think that they should be allowed to stay if they’re good people, working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.”

The president later went on to characterize his immigration policy as “too tough” and expressed interest in working across the aisle in the next Congress, when both chambers will be under Democratic control.

Deportations have been a key focus for the second Trump administration – but it may have cost Trump politically.

In a July survey the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research found that 39 percent of respondents approved of the administration’s handling of immigration, a 10-point drop from the start of his second term.

Americans have developed increasingly negative views of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), especially following the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti earlier this year in Minneapolis, which led to widespread backlash and protests nationwide .

Many Democratic lawmakers have condemned the president’s action on immigration – but some Republican lawmakers have also shared their concerns and foresaw the president’s immigration crackdown as a liability.

“Once you start deporting people who have otherwise been here without incident for 15, 20 years, that’s a gray zone that I think where you find a lot of division of opinion,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said in early October.

Cornyn was up for re-election but lost the Republican primary to Trump-backed Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton. He was defeated on Tuesday by the now Sen.-elect James Talarico (D-Texas), who was critical of ICE’s actions throughout his campaign..

“We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that’s not what we’re seeing,” Talarico said at a town hall in October. “What we’ve seen over the last year is a secret police force, and that’s what we don’t want in this country.”
